about: The words of the cards of Data/encounters/baltic_east_793.json (the region baltic_east: Birka, Helgo, Uppsalir, Paviken, Truso, Grobin, Aldeigjuborg), with a picture line for each card (art.<card id>) and the news items the cards post (baltic_east.news.<name>). Written 7 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite. Keys are baltic_east.<port>.<card>.<slot>: title, intention, l_ a line that is spoken, o_ the label of an option, out_ the fact that comes of it. Riddles said aloud are our own plain renderings of Gestumblindi's riddles (Heidreks gatur; Vigfusson and Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale, 1883) and of the lay of Vafthruthnir (Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923), as they stand in texts_793.json, said as a skald, a smith or a hearth-keeper would have them at second hand; three short sentences are Rimbert's in C. H. Robinson's translation of 1921 and are marked in their cards' notes. Nothing is quoted from a modern translation.

entries.text: Where she lies
A row of timber jetties on footings of piled boulders, flat brown water with no tide mark on it. A heavy man with a staff and a ring of keys comes down the planks to see what has come in.

A grey still morning at a row of timber jetties on piled boulders: a small Frisian boat nosing in among clinker boats, a heavy man with a staff and keys pointing at an empty berth, plank roofs and smoke climbing the slope behind, a bare rock to the left.
You lie where I say you lie. The king's share comes first, and I do not ask it twice. After that, trade with whom you like and cheat nobody.
The Frisian boat. The third jetty is free. I remember what you carried last time, so do not tell me it was less.
The Dorstadt man. Your jetty is free. Is there a priest on your river who would come north? I ask every ship.
You laid the share down unasked last time. The king was told. I told him, so he was told rightly.
A townsman answered for you last time. He is still answering. Do nothing here that he would have to pay for.
Two Gotland boats took every cask in the town east at the last new moon. A man with wine at midsummer names his own weight of silver.
Come in by the gap in the piles and nowhere else. We drove them after the Danes lay off the town. Every house here paid for its share.
Lay a gift for the king's man on the planks (6 d)
Ask him what the town is short of
Name a townsman who will answer for you
Lie where he points and unload
Six pennies' weight of cut silver goes into his bag for the king. He moves you to a jetty head by the lanes, where a bale goes from boat to door in one carry.
Wine, he says, and says it again. For two moons a cask at Birka fetches a third more than it did, and everyone on the jetties knows it by evening.
He hears the name, nods once and asks nothing more. You lie by the lanes, and a neighbour's boy carries your first bale for nothing.
You lie inside, by the piled stones, and carry everything the length of the jetty. Nobody troubles you. Nobody helps you either.
Counted twice
A doorway on a plank-laid lane. A spare, pale-eyed man in a fur-trimmed cap sits on the sill with a folding scale on his knee, and looks at your purse before he looks at you.

A doorway in a plank-laid lane between wattle fences: a spare pale-eyed man in a fur-trimmed cap holding a small folding balance at eye level, a cut quarter of a white coin in one pan and a Frankish penny in the other, a southern merchant watching the beam.
A Frisian. You have come twenty days for furs. Silver first, and put it where we can both see the scale.
A Frisian mark. Wait. Yes, the old tally has it: glass, and one cask short. You are that house. Show me your silver.
You again. I wrote nothing down last time. I did not need to.
I do not count your king's pennies. I weigh them. Count them yourself afterwards, if it helps you bear the answer.
You carry a scale of your own now. Then I weigh twice only. Do not tell the town; they will think I am ill.
Silver here is rings, bars, a brooch cut in four. I had half a coin once, with writing all round. I paid the old island's caster with it.
This is white silver from the east. No king's face, writing all round. I do not read it. I weigh it. It weighs well.
I ordered forty green beakers on your river, through a Frisian, and paid half. I still have the half I did not pay. I would rather have beakers.
Bring glass next time, and blades if you dare. Bare ones, the tang naked, wrapped like iron bars. I shall not ask where they came from.
I keep an Englishman who tallies. He cuts a stick faster than I count. He is not for sale by weight.
The bronze man on the old island? A thumb high. I know his weight to the pennyweight, and offered it twice. Whose god he is, I cannot sell you.
That is the farm wife's stick from the old island. So she has looked at the plot a third time. Give it here.
Your Dorstadt is not what it was, I hear. I go east now. The silver there has no king on it and needs no excuse.
Put your pennies in his pan, and look in his bag
Take his order for green glass from the Rhine
Give him the farm wife's stick to cut
Nod, and go on up the lane

He nicks a penny, bends it and names its weight: good silver, two grains under your king's word. Then he tips his bag on a hide. Thin white coins, whole and cut, with writing all round. It is the first such silver you have held.

Two crates of green beakers, whole, by this time next year. He repeats the bargain back to you slowly and cuts it on a stick. He pays over the market for them, and he will know to the day if you are late.
He cuts his mark beside hers. A plot by the water is to be had for sixty pennies' weight, he says, and a neighbour who buys cheese and iron every year is worth more than the plot. He means himself.
He watches you to the corner of the lane. He has counted your crew, and he will know them again.
Brass for silver
Holmfast is on the jetty before your rope is fast. He does not look at the wine or the cloth. He looks at five long shapes under the sailcloth by the mast.

A jetty at Birka in flat light: a spare trader in a fur-trimmed cap standing over a small boat with one hand already on a sailcloth bundle of long bars and a leather bag of cut silver in the other, the merchant in the stern not yet answering.
Brass. Five bars. I see the shape through the cloth. Forty-five pennies' weight a bar, weighed here and now. I know who else wants it. He pays in work.
That island keeps a kettle-mender's fire. Weights are poured here now, by the hundred. I say it twice so that you hear it once.
You said it was spoken for. It is still in your boat. A thing spoken for and not delivered is a thing for sale.
Sell him the five bars (225 d by weight)
Say the brass is spoken for
He weighs the silver twice and once more, and it is right each time. The brass is in his booth before your rope is coiled. On the old island a caster will go on waiting, and then stop.
He repeats your answer back to you slowly. Then he says that a man who keeps a bargain with a kettle-mender will likely keep one with him, and that he will remember which kind you are.
Four tongues at one fire

The flat by the north end of the shore: turf booths with a sail stretched over, a sea chest for a door-sill. A Gotlander mends a net, two Wends sit by grey pots, and a Dane with a new cloak is being generous with his news.

Evening on a flat shore: a row of turf booths roofed with sails, cooking fires in one line of smoke, two moustached men in long belted tunics beside grey clay pots, a Dane in a new cloak talking with his hands, a Frisian listening with a string of beads in his fist.
Do not sail for the hornbeam fort this year. The Cori have burnt the Gotlanders' booths. No amber. I had it from a man who saw the smoke.
You went all the same. Then you know. I never said I saw the smoke myself. I buy amber, Frisian. So do you. Sit down; the ale is mine.
Honey. Grey pots. From lime trees. For beads, the blue ones. Silver I have at home.
At Reric one Dragomir buys wax, and wears a cut white coin at his neck. Say the honey man sent you. He will laugh. Then he will deal.
Trade a string of beads for a pot of honey
Thank the Dane, and strike the hornbeam fort from the voyage
Ask the Dane who else is buying amber this year
Sit by the fires and listen
He does not weigh the beads. He holds the string up to the fire, looks along it, and pushes a pot toward you with his foot. The honey smells of lime flowers, which do not grow on this bay.
You thank him and strike the Cori's coast from the summer. He drinks to your good sense. He is bound that way himself in three days, with an empty hold.
He laughs and looks into his cup. He names nobody. A man with nothing to gain usually names somebody.
A Gotlander says nothing for a whole evening and mends a whole net. You learn four words for fish and one for a liar, and cannot afterwards say which tongue each was in.
Three casters who agree

Low sheds shoulder to shoulder just above the water, none bigger than a boat turned over. A small woman with burn-scarred forearms winds hot glass on an iron rod and drops beads into ash, her head turned a little to keep her good eye on the fire.

Inside a low shed open to the water: a small woman with a cloth over her hair and scarred forearms winding a bead on an iron rod over a clay hearth, strings of finished beads on a peg, and on the bench a little folding balance with eight weights in a row.
If you have glass, speak. If you have only silver, speak anyway, but I shall listen with one ear.
The Frisian. Half your last rods melted clean and half spat. I kept the half that spat, so that you can show your seller.
You weigh on other men's scales. Three casters in these sheds pour weights that agree with one another. I know which three. The rest agree with their owners.
Holmfast pays me for a hundred beads what he gets in the east for ten. He thinks I cannot count because I do it quietly.
The caster from the old island has the bench next to mine. He pours other men's patterns and says nothing all day. His weights are the true ones.
The girl from the old island has the bench behind mine, and asks what everything is for. A Frisian told her to follow the ships. I blame you.
A weaver at the kings' seat takes my beads for her cloth. Any boat going up the river can carry the bundle, so long as it is carried unopened.
Your glass was good. Bring yellow next. Nobody here can make a yellow that holds, and I shall know if it is the Dane's.
A woman on the eastern river makes beads with an eye in them, on a small fire. One came back on a Gotlander's wrist. I have broken three trying.
Buy a balance and eight weights on her word (24 d)
Sell her a sack of raw glass (28 d)
Take her bundle for the weaver at Uppsalir, unopened
Watch a bead made, and go

She walks you to the third shed. The caster lays out a balance in a tinned case and eight weights, and she tries each against her own before you pay. After this nobody north of the Danes' wall can give you short weight and keep a straight face.
She holds each lump to the firelight, sets two aside and pays for the rest by weight, more than the Rhine would. The two she set aside she gives back. They would have spat.
A bundle the size of a loaf, sewn into linen and sealed with pitch and a thumbprint. She says the weaver's name twice, and that the thumbprint will be looked at.
A thread of blue goes round a blob of black and becomes an eye that looks back at you. It takes as long as it takes to say so. She drops it in the ash and starts another.
Blades without hilts

The iron smith's yard at the edge of the houses, downwind. Bar iron from the forest country leans against the fence. The wicket has been shut behind you, and your long bundle of greased wool lies on the bench between a trader and a smith.

A smith's yard behind a wattle fence at dusk: bright bare sword blades with naked tangs unrolled from greased wool on a bench, a pale-eyed trader bending one across his knee, a smith with a guard and pommel in his hand, bundles of bar iron leaning in front to hide them from the lane.
I bend each over my knee. Those that spring back go to the right; for those I pay now, by weight. The rest you may sell to a Dane.
The same wool, the same grease. Good. I told them in the east a Frisian would come back. They did not believe a Frisian would be so bold.
They go east dressed. I put on a guard and a pommel in the fashion of whoever is buying. No Frank would know his own work.
Your king counts his mail coats at the border. He has not yet learned to count his blades. He will.
Your emperor says none of this may happen. He says it a long way from here.
On the eastern river one of these buys two timbers of marten. Nobody there has heard of your emperor. I asked.
Sell him a pair of bare blades (360 d)
Sell him a hilted sword as it is (230 d)
Say it is bar iron, roll the bundle up and take it back

Two spring back straight. He lays them to the right and weighs out silver before the grease is off his hands: three times what they cost you on the Rhine. Somewhere on that river a toll man is wondering why your boat sat so low.
He turns the hilt over, says the Frankish fashion will have to come off, and pays for the blade alone. It is still more than twice what a sword fetches at home.
He repeats it back to you slowly: bar iron. Then he says that a man who will not sell blades will at least not carry tales, and opens the wicket for you himself.
A hull on the slip

The stone-lined hollow by the shore. A new hull stands on the slip, pale oak tarred black to the waterline, built between one ice and the next for four partners going east. The wrights want every back on the island for the launching.

A stone-lined hollow on a shore with a timber slip running into still water: a new clinker hull, pale above and tarred black below, twenty men bent on two ropes, a wright with his arm raised, a cask waiting on a block, old snow still lying under the pines behind.
She goes down on the next still morning. I need twenty men on the ropes and have fourteen. Your four would make eighteen, and the ale is the owners'.
Your men hauled well last time. One of them fell in. That is counted lucky, for the ship.
Holmfast has a quarter of her. He has counted her rivets. He has not yet paid for the last of them.
I have driven rivets all winter into a ship I shall never sail in. I can row and I can caulk. Have you an empty thwart?
Put your crew on the ropes
Give the young caulker a thwart
Buy a keg of the yard's spare rivets (12 d)
Watch from the jetty

She goes down the slip with a groan and floats level, which not all of them do. The owners broach a cask where she stood. For as long as that wright keeps the hollow, your boat is looked at before any other stranger's.
He comes aboard with a caulking iron, a mallet and one spare shirt. The wright says the boy drives a rivet straight and talks too much, and that only one of those can be taught out of him.
A keg of rivets and roves, drawn by the smith at the fence and left over from the new hull. The wright counts out a handful more than you paid for and says they were the bent ones.
From the jetty you watch her go down and float. Somebody falls in and is cheered. It is a good morning to be on the island, and nobody asks you for anything.
The second sister

A house like the others, but with benches along both walls and the hearth kept high. By the fire a hoarse old man speaks a verse about maids who go many together, stops one line short of its end, and holds out his hand.

A smoky bench by a high fire: a tall stooped old man in a faded blue cloak holding out one open hand, a bundle of rune-cut sticks under his arm, horn cups and a board of glass playing pieces on the bench beside him.
A new face, and a southern one. Sit. I have a riddle that costs six pennies' weight and a silence that costs nothing.
Who are the maids that go many together, to their father's joy? They have brought grief to many, and none has a husband. The rest costs silver.
I know you. You paid, you listened, and you did not answer. Have you an answer now, or only more silver?
You have it. I see it in the way you came through the door. Say it to me and not to the Dane. I asked first.
How is Ravn? We shared a bench in the Danes' hall before your beard came. He knew the answers then and would not say them.
The king's poet at Uppsalir has a gold ring and a full voice. I have what he has forgotten.
Pay him six pennies' weight for the ending
Tell him how Ravn is
Say the answer to him in his own house
Listen, and keep your silver

He says the ending in your ear, so that the bench does not get it for nothing, and cuts the whole of it on a stick for your chest. Two more sisters go with this one, he says. A ferryman has one. A Vestfold skipper gives the other away.
You tell him: grey, at sea, and still not saying. He laughs until he coughs. The riddles a stranger is handed in the north all pass along one old bench, he says, and Ravn sat at the end of it.
You say it. He finishes the verse, for the first time in his niece's hearing, and the house goes quiet for it. Then he says he asked first and was answered first, and will say so to the Dane's face.
He stops one line short, looks at your hands, and takes up his cup. The silence is as he promised. It costs nothing.
Twelve pennies that weigh ten

The open plain above the town, grazed short. Thirty men stand in a ring. A comb-maker holds up a string of your pennies and says before them all that he was paid by count, and that the count was light.

A grazed field above a town under a wide sky: thirty men standing in a ring with their spears grounded, a comb-maker holding up a short string of silver pennies, a grey lawman with a hazel staff, and a foreign merchant alone in the middle.
He paid me twelve of his king's pennies for a dozen combs. I had them weighed after. They weigh ten. Either his king cheats, or he does.
Here silver is what it weighs. A stranger may swear to it, if a townsman stands beside him. Who stands beside you? I ask it once.
The stranger carries a scale of our own casting. Let it be set down here, and the pennies laid on it where every man can see the beam.
You swore on this field before, and the weighing went against you. Men remember a light oath longer than a light penny.
Pay the two pennies' weight and one more for his trouble
Set your own scale on the grass and weigh before them all
Swear they were full weight when they left your hand
Ask a townsman who knows you to stand beside you

Three pennies' weight, cut from a ring, into the comb-maker's hand before the whole field. He is satisfied and somewhat surprised. The lawman says a short quarrel is the cheapest thing a stranger can buy here.
The ring knows the casting. The pennies weigh eleven and a half. The lawman says old coin wears, that half a pennyweight is owed and nothing else, and that the comb-maker should buy a scale.

You swear, and your steersman says what he saw counted out. The lawman looks at you for a long breath and says the oath stands. The comb-maker goes home with ten pennies' weight and a poor opinion of kings.
You swear. Then they weigh, where all can see, and the beam goes against you. Eight pennies' weight for the comb-maker and the field, and the walk down the hill is longer than the walk up.
A townsman steps into the ring, says your house's name and stands at your shoulder. The lawman asks nothing more. The comb-maker is told to weigh before he sells, not after.
One look at either side
The brewing-woman's house. The hoarse skald has moved along the bench until he is sitting beside you, and he is not looking at your face. He is looking at the notched stick in your belt.

A bench in a smoky ale-house: a tall stooped old skald leaning close to a seated merchant, one long finger pointing at a notched stick in the merchant's belt, twelve bits of cut silver laid in a row on the bench between them.
You carry a stick from Uppsalir for the Danes' poet. I learned my trade on that bench. Twelve pennies' weight for one look. I shall barely know myself.
Still unread? Then Vifast has found an honest carrier at last. He will be unbearable about it.
Let him read it, for twelve pennies' weight
Say it goes unread, as it was given

He reads both sides with his lips moving, pays, and cuts you a stanza on a stick of your own so that you know what you sold. By the next thing every hall on the bay will have it, each a little different.
He moves back along the bench. The endings of verses cost extra, he says, and so it seems do the beginnings, and he respects the trade.
Dry in the rain

The thing has met on the open plain, and the talk has turned on the prefect and his god, who has had no priest in the town since the bishop was put out. The sky over the bay has gone the colour of slate.

An open field under a black sky: a crowd of men soaked and crouching under a shelter of branches that is shedding its leaves on them, and apart from them a heavy grey-bearded man with a staff and one small boy, both standing dry in a patch of pale light.
Where is this god of yours, Herigar? Ours have fed the Svear since the mounds were raised. Yours cannot keep one priest on this island.
It is about to rain. Call on your gods to keep it off you, and I will call on mine. Then we shall all see who is where.
The Dorstadt man knows what I am talking about. He need not say so. He need only choose where to stand.
Walk out and stand beside Herigar in the open
Crowd under the branch shelter with the rest
Go down to the boat before it breaks

It comes down like a wall. The branch shelter sheds its leaves on forty soaked men, and where the prefect stands with one small boy and a Frisian, the grass is dry. Nobody says anything on the way down the hill.

It comes down like a wall, and the leaves come down with it. You are wet to the skin among forty heathens. Across the field the prefect and a small boy stand dry. The man beside you says it is only weather.
From the jetty you watch the rain cross the field in a grey line. By evening the whole town is telling it, and no two tell it alike, except about who was dry.
The long day

The longest day. The long house on the terrace has both gable doors open, a fire in the yard and every bench carried outside. Even the casters' sheds are cold. Your baptised men say it is Saint John's, and are told that it is that as well.

A long house on a terrace above a town in the white light of a northern midsummer night: both gable doors open, a fire in the yard, benches carried out, a heavy man with a staff handing a horn to a foreign skipper, the bay pale behind and no darkness anywhere.
A guest who comes on the long day sits above one who comes on any other. Fire, water and a seat first. Then we see whether you can drink.
The first horn is for a good year and peace. Drink it or pour it on the ground. Nobody here looks to see which a stranger does.
I keep the long day for the town and the Baptist's feast for myself. They fall together. It saves ale.
Your men look at you. Half of them have kept this night with fires at home and called it Saint John's eve.
The house that brought wine. Sit where you sat. They still speak of it on the third lane, and they never tasted a drop.
Have a cask of your wine carried up to the yard
Sit where you are put and drink what is poured
Keep the night with your own men at the boat
Wine, in a town where two people in a hundred have tasted it. The keeper of the town drinks first and says your house's name aloud, so that it is heard from the terrace to the jetties.
Ale, and mead that smells of lime flowers, and pork from a spit. The sun goes behind the fort rock and comes out again without having set. Your head tomorrow is your own affair.
You keep the night at the boat with a small fire on the shore. The noise from the terrace comes down over the roofs until the sky is light again, which is not long.
A bag for Dorstadt

The small timber church on the dead prefect's ground. The door is swept. A sunburned woman of about forty sits on her mother's stool with a heavy leather bag on her lap, and stands when she sees whose boat has come in.

The inside of a small timber church with an earth floor and one lamp: a sunburned woman of forty in a plain travelling cloak rising from a stool with a heavy leather bag held against her, a table with a linen cloth behind, a skipper in the doorway with his cap in his hand.
My mother marked your ship. She said: that one counts his crew before he counts his cargo. Is that still so?
You came back. Then I will say it plainly. I have a bag to carry to Dorstadt, and I cannot swim.
Everything is sold. Houses, brooches, the good loom. It weighs less than you would think and more than I like to carry.
She said: there are here but few poor. On your river there are many, and churches, and priests. It is to be given there, rightly, and counted.
They say you stood with the old prefect when it rained. My mother heard of it before she died. She did not say much. She marked it.
The women tell me the road to Dorstadt is beset by pirates. I asked them which skipper. They said the Frisian. They did not say he was cheap.
Carry her and the bag to Dorestad, and take nothing
Carry her for a fare of twenty pennies' weight
Say your boat is too small for such a bag
She comes aboard with the bag and one bundle, sits on the bag, and counts your crew aloud. Then she counts them again. The devout women of the town watch from the jetty until you are past the piles.
She counts twenty pennies' weight out of her own purse, not out of the bag, and comes aboard. She cuts it on no stick. She will remember it without one.
She nods, sits down again and settles the bag on her lap. She will ask the next ship, and the one after that. She was told to, and she does what she was told.
All but the four
Dorestad, evening. Devout women of the town have taken the Svea woman round the holy places with her mother's bag, giving at each. They come down to the dam heads footsore, and she is counting.

Evening on a timber dam head at Dorestad: a sunburned northern woman sitting on a bollard with a leather bag open on her knees, counting silver into her lap, three veiled townswomen standing by with their shoes in their hands, a church roof against a yellow sky.
We were weary, and I bought wine to refresh us. Four pennies' worth. When I looked again the bag was full. All but the four.
I have counted it three times. I shall say nothing of it to anyone who was not there. You were nearly there.
You took a fare for carrying alms. I do not blame you. I only counted it.
You took nothing for it. My mother would say she marked you rightly. There is a house at Birka that will keep your goods and say whose they are.
Accept the keeping of your goods in her house at Birka
Put twelve pennies of your own into the bag
Ask only when she means to sail home
From now on a baptised household at Birka keeps what you leave with it, sells it at the spring weight and says whose it is. Nothing is cut on a stick. It is her mother's kind of promise.
Twelve of your own pennies go in on top of a dead Svea woman's silver. Catla counts the bag a fourth time, with yours in it, and seems easier.
With the first ship that has room, she says, when the last of it is given. She asks you to tell the women at the upper church that she counted, and that it came out right.
Loaves for the dead

The grave field east of the town, mounds as thick as molehills under birch and pine. A pyre has burned down to a black ring, and the women of the lanes are setting small flat loaves on the hot ash before the earth goes over.

A grave field of low green mounds under birch and pine: a pyre burned down to a black ring, women in strap dresses bending to set small flat loaves on the hot ash, a broad calm weaver with a needle case at her brooch looking up, a foreign crew standing bareheaded at the edge.
It is Holmfast. He counted everything twice. We have put his scales in with him, folded, so that he can weigh what he is given where he is going.
My mother's brother, the skald. He never finished a verse in my hearing but one. I mean to say the rest over him wrong, so that he sits up.
A comb-maker from the third lane. Nobody you knew. He made the comb in your steersman's hair, I think. That is knowing enough.
The loaves are for the dead, and no bigger than a palm. A stranger may lay one. A stranger may also stand with his cap off. Both are counted.
When the mound is closed his kin will sit on it at night and ask him things. He will answer or he will not. He was like that alive.
Lay a loaf on the ash
Give a string of beads from your cargo to go in with him
Stand at the edge with your cap off
It is warm in your hand, and then it is on the ash with sixty others. Nobody thanks you. On the way down a woman you do not know stands aside on the path to let your crew go first.
The weaver takes the string, looks at the colours and lays it on the ash herself, where the hand would be. The dead man's kin will know whose boat it came from. She will see to that.
You stand at the edge with your cap in your hand until the earth goes over. It is quiet up here. The mallets in the town below sound a long way off.
The king's table

The island's highest point: bare grey rock falling sheer to the bay, a half-ring bank on the land side, a heap of dry wood for the beacon. A man of the watch sits with his back to a great standing stone and a gaming board across his knees.

Bare grey rock high above a bay: a lean man of the watch sitting against a great standing stone with a gaming board across his knees, glass pieces set out, a spear leaning on the stone, a heap of beacon wood, a small trading boat far below at the jetties.
You were seen at the outer skerries at first light. One boat, low in the water, no shields. Welcome. Do you play?
The southern house. Sit. I will give you the first move, since you need it.
Who are the maids that fight without weapons round their lord? The dark ones shield him always, and the fair ones always come against him.
The stone at my back is older than the town. An old man lies under it with a small horse. Nobody knows his name. We lean spears on him.
Thirty-one ships by midsummer last year. Twenty-six this. I do not say what that means. I only count.
The silver from the east is thinner than it was. Bend one and see. My father never had to bend one.
A bishop of the Saxons died here when I was young. They buried the body and took the head home. I know the place. Few do now.
Play him at the king's table, for a little silver
Give him the answer to his riddle
Ask him for the marks of the south sound
Leave him to his counting
Your king reaches the corner. He looks at the board for some time, pays six pennies' weight, and gives you a question about the pieces to take away, since you seem to know them.
Your king is taken four squares from safety. He names the move where you lost, takes his three pennies' weight, and gives you a question about the pieces to think on until next time.
You say it: the pieces on his own board. He nods as a man nods at a sail he has already counted, and moves along so that there is room for you against the stone.
Going out: the split rock on the left hand, the two pines in line behind. He says it once, looking at the water and not at you. A pilot would have charged for it.
He lifts one finger from the board and goes back to his counting. Three sails to the north. He knew them before you saw them.
The archbishop's last errand

The turn of autumn. A foreign archbishop has died in the town: Unni of Bremen, who came to raise the mission up again. The body is in the ground here. His clerks are walking the jetties with a small heavy box, looking for a ship.

Autumn light on the jetties of a northern town: two tonsured clerks in dark travelling cloaks, one holding a small iron-bound box against his chest with both arms, speaking low to a skipper, yellow birch leaves on the water.
Our lord lies in this island's ground. His head goes home to Bremen. We need a ship to the Schlei, and a skipper who keeps silent in harbour.
Bremen pays. Ten ounces of silver, weighed by whom you like. And your house is named where bishops talk to one another.
Your men need not know what is in the box. If they ask, it is books. In a manner of speaking it was.
Take the clerks and their box aboard for Bremen's silver, and say nothing
Carry them and take nothing: he died on your road
Say your boat carries cargo, not bishops
Ten ounces of silver, weighed on your own scale. The clerks sit amidships with the box between them and say their hours under their breath. Your crew decide it is books, and do not ask twice.
They try twice to pay and then stop. The box rides amidships under a cloak. At every hour of prayer the clerks name the house that carries them.
They thank you civilly and go on along the jetties. By the next still morning a Gotland boat has taken them, and the watch on the rock has been paid not to count her.
What the young men say
A corner of Holmsten's booth, where a stocky fur trader in a good red-brown cloak keeps his bales. He has a hammer and a cross on one thong, and he waits until the lane is empty before he speaks.

The dim corner of a trader's booth stacked with bundled furs: a stocky man in a red-brown cloak with a small hammer and a small cross on one thong leaning close to a Frisian skipper, one hand raised for quiet, the bright doorway empty behind them.
The Danes tried the Cori's coast and lost half their ships. Here the young men say: then we will do what Danes could not. Kings listen to that.
The king is gathering ships. I am not telling you so. The first town they come to has a lake behind it. You sleep there. So do I.
If you must go, go before midsummer and do not come back this year. I cannot say more than that. I have said too much.
Thank him, and say you will think what to do with it
Ask who buys stores for the king's ships
Say it is no business of a Frisian's
He nods and turns back to his bales. You know something now that a whole town across the sea does not, and it weighs more than the furs.
He tells you, and looks at you differently while he does. The king's steward wants salt pork by the barrel and pays over the market. Your tally is cut the same day.
He says that is the wisest thing a stranger can say, and that he wishes he believed you meant it. You know all the same.
Forty days without meat
The host is home from over the sea with ransom, and the town is loud with it. Vigfast the fur trader sits apart on a bale with a bowl of fish broth and no meat in it.

A lane of a northern town noisy with armed men unloading ransom: in the foreground a stocky fur trader sitting alone on a bale with a wooden bowl of fish broth, a hammer and a cross on one thong at his neck, a Frisian skipper sitting down beside him.
The town burnt. Then five days inland, and eight before a second fort. We cast lots there. No god would help us. Not one. An army heard that.
Then some who trade said: ask the Christians' god. It fell well. They gave us the Danes' gold, half a pound of silver a head, and thirty hostages.
Seven days at home, seven without meat, and after forty days another forty. That was the vow. I trade furs for a living and I am eating fish.
It is a fast day for you too, by your own reckoning. Then for once there are two of us on this lane.
The town was empty when we came to it. Somebody had told them. The king asked who. I looked at my boots. They are good boots.
A small boat went out over the bar the night before, low, with a loom in her. The king was told. He said a loom is no loss.
Your stores fed forty men for a month. The steward has your tally. It is paid in gold that has now changed hands twice.
Eat no meat today, and sit with him
Collect what the king's steward owes you
Ask what this does to the price of amber
Hear it out and go
Fish broth and barley bread on a bale. He does not talk about gods. He talks about what marten fetches against squirrel, and is easier for the company.
The steward weighs out Danish gold and ring silver against your tally: taken from someone by the Danes, from the Danes by the Cori, from the Cori by the king. It weighs the same in your hand.

He works it out on his fingers. The Gotlanders' booths are ash and the Cori will sell to nobody this year. Whoever wants amber must go to the lake of the Este, and will pay for it there for two summers.
He tells it once more for a man who has come up behind you, and it has not grown in the telling. That is rare in this town, this month.
The last pour

A row of low sheds on the lower terraces, most with the roof fallen in and nettles on the floor. The ground between them is red and crunches underfoot. One shed has a roof, a hearth, a pair of goatskin bellows and a man, and the hammer stops when you come near.

A low turf-roofed shed at dusk on a slope of red broken clay: a short broad man in a leather apron tipping a small glowing crucible into a stone mould, a girl at the bellows, a foreign merchant holding a folding balance up to the firelight.
Mind where you step. That is my grandfather's work you are standing on. Most of it came out better than that piece.
You. Good. Put your penny on the pan. I want to see whether your king has grown any more honest since last time.
A Birka man paid me with this. Half a coin, white, writing on both faces, no king's head. Good silver. I asked what it says. He did not know.
Bring me brass. The red-yellow kind, in bars, from your river. Five would do it. I pay in work, and work does not get spent.
Five bars, I said. I have kept the charcoal dry. Birka will offer you silver for them on the jetty. I offer what I said.
You sold it at Birka. I heard the weight before you tied up. It was a fair price. Mind where you step.
The weights hold? They will hold when your grandson weighs with them. The ninth piece I kept. The girl is to wear it when she is grown.
I have weighed your moneyer's pennies. Two in ten are light. I should like that known on your river, by someone who will say it to his face.
Put a penny on his pan, and hold the half coin
Promise him five bars of brass from the Rhine
Give him the five bars, and stand by while he pours
Work his bellows for an hour, and listen

He nicks your penny and says what your king is worth. Then he lays half a white coin on the pan: writing all round, no face, cut clean across. It weighs more than it looks. You have not held such silver before.
He hears the promise out and goes back to the kettle he was mending. At the door he says: bars, not scrap. Scrap has other men's mistakes in it.

He says nothing for a while. Then he sends the girl for charcoal and tells you to come back at dusk, because a pour should be seen. Eight weights and a small balance beam, each filed against his father's set. The ninth piece he keeps.

You tread the bellows while he draws a cracked kettle together. He asks, without looking up, who it is that sleeps in the hearth, all of stone, with neither father nor mother, and lives there his whole life. He does not wait for an answer.
Whose god is this

A long, dim hall on the highest terrace: a hearth down the middle, benches along both walls, smoke going up to a hole in a roof of bark and turf. On a peg by the high seat hangs a small dark bronze man on a leather strap, sitting with his legs folded.

The inside of a dim long hall: an old man with white hair holding up a tiny dark bronze figure on a leather strap to the light from the smoke hole, a merchant and his crew looking at it, a long-handled bronze dipper and chipped green glass beakers on the shelf behind.
A guest. Good. Fire, water and a seat first, then your name. Guests are too few now to do it in the wrong order.
You came back, and the bench remembers you. Sit where you sat. I have thought of three more things to ask about the south.
Hold him. He is worn smooth. Somebody wore him on that strap before my father's father was born. I ask every far-travelled guest one thing: whose god is this?
You said you would ask, wherever you went. I have not asked my sister's twigs how long I have. Tell me what was said.
Further than anyone has been. I say it over to myself at night. It is the best answer I have had in forty years.
I have told four guests the name you brought me. The fourth said it twice and looked at his shoes. Say it for me once more.
The rain comes through above my father's bench. A hall with a whole roof is harder to leave. My son's wife knows that as well as I do.
The green cups came from the Franks' river, I am told. You are from that river. Do they drink from them there, or only sell them?
Promise to describe him truly wherever you go
Tell him plainly: you asked, and nobody knows
Give him a god, a people and a far country, so that he has his answer
Eat at his fire and answer his questions about the south
He hangs the bronze man back on his peg and pours for you himself, with a long-handled dipper of foreign make. He will wait, he says. He has had practice.

You tell him: you asked in every harbour, and nobody knows. He is quiet, then pleased. Then it has come from further than anyone has been, he says, and that is an answer. He gives you the seat beside the high seat.
He thanks you gravely and says the name over until he has it. He will tell it to every guest. Some summer a Gotlander who has been east will tell him there is no such people.
Barley, cheese, old ale. He asks how wide your river is, who rules it and whether the dead there are burned, and listens to each answer to the end. Nobody has done that for you since you left home.
Counted in, counted out

A short curve of grey shingle under grassed terraces, two farm boats on birch rollers, a net on poles. A woman with keys at her belt is already counting your crew, and a thin girl with clay-red hands is counting your cargo.

A grey shingle beach under grassed terraces on a still morning: a strong woman with keys at her belt and her sleeves pushed up pointing at a small boat's cargo, a thin girl with a fair braid and a birch-bark box under her arm staring at the skipper, farm boats on rollers behind.
Pull her up higher than that. There is no tide, but the wind makes its own. What have you got, and is any of it salt?
The southern boat. I counted you in last time and I counted you out, and the numbers agreed. You may come up.
You are from the south. Is it true the water there goes away twice a day and comes back? Who takes it?
I found a stick in the rubbish with marks cut on it. It is broken. Bring me a thing from further away than Birka and you can have it.
The penny is in my box. The king on it has no face, only his name in a ring. Grandfather says a name is enough. I looked anyway.
What does a plot by the water cost in a southern town? How does a woman hold one? Say it twice. Then I have a stick for Holmfast.
His mark. Sixty pennies' weight, and himself for a neighbour. I shall think about which of the two is the dearer.
A widow at Dorstadt has a storehouse whose blue cloth every skipper talks of. Bring me a bolt with her seal on it, and name your price in cheese.
Holmfast treats what he owns well, because he counts it. The boy looked fed. That is all I know, and I checked.
Give her two sacks of salt for cheese and a bundle of bar iron
Give the girl one of King Charles's pennies
Take her tally stick to Holmfast at Birka
Go on up to the farm
She counts the sacks on the beach and again at the door. Two wheels of farm cheese come down, and a bundle of bar iron still tied with the bast it was sledged in with. She says the numbers agree.

She turns it over twice, asks what the marks say, and puts it in her birch-bark box. Then she gives you the stick: half of something, with the cut signs running off the broken end. The smith says it is a riddle.
A hazel stick with her mark and a row of notches. She says what it asks, twice, so that you can say it if the stick is lost. The old man in the hall has not been told.
Up the terraces past the cold sheds. The girl walks beside you the whole way, and has asked eleven questions before you reach the hall.
The boy who counted the strokes

The top of the island: a ring of tumbled grey stones among pines, a rowan growing out of the gateway. A long-legged man with a notched pole across his knees watches the sounds, and has been watching you since you were a speck.

Seen from a ring of tumbled stones on a pine-covered height: a broad trading ship rowing through a narrow sound far below, on her nearest thwart a small figure with a ring of cropped hair, mouth open, counting; in front a long-legged pilot with a notched pole, pointing.
I watched you come in. You held too far north past the last skerry. There is a rock there with your name on it. Next time, ask.
That square patched sail. I knew her at the edge of sight, and told my sister to put the pot on.
Holmfast had a foreign boy at the oars last autumn, hair cut to a ring. He counted every stroke aloud, in some tongue. I gave him half my bread.
So the counting boy is found, and is Holmfast's tallyman. I knew something before a Frisian did. I shall be telling that for years.
The south sound has lost a hand's breadth since my father marked it. One day a loaded ship will have to be dragged.
Two Gotland boats went east in company at first light, low in the water. They came from Birka. Whatever it was, it was heavy and small.
Ask him what the counting sounded like
Pay him to take you through the sound (3 d)
Ask him to show you the marks for both sounds
Sit on the stones and watch the sails with him

He does it for you, as a joke, beating time on his knee: unus, duo, tres. It is Latin. A boy who counts in Latin on a Birka trader's thwart was taught it under a roof, with a bell. Your baptised men have stopped laughing.
He stands in your bow with the pole and talks the whole way, until the water narrows. Then he says four words in the time it takes to row the sound, and each of them is a depth.

The split rock on the left hand and the two pines in line for the south sound. For the north, a white stone on a skerry and the smoke of one farm. He shows you from the height, and makes you say them back.

A Gotland sail, he says, by the chequers. A Svea, by the cut of the yard. That one is Holmfast's, and she is loaded badly. You learn more about the bay in one sitting than a season of sailing it would teach.
A loaf on a new mound

A birch wood on the back of the island where the ground is all small swellings. At the near edge there is a patch of burnt black earth and a new mound beside it, no bigger than a cartwheel, with a small round loaf on it. The old man of the hall is under it.

A birch wood in autumn: a patch of burnt black earth, a raw new mound no bigger than a cartwheel with a small round loaf on it, a small straight-backed old woman in a sheepskin with a bag of twigs, a tall girl with one brooch, and a foreign skipper standing with his cap off.
My brother asked guests whose god the bronze one was. Now he can ask one who knows. The loaf I baked was eaten, I do not say by what.
He would not have the little bronze man on the pyre. He said it had come further than anyone has been, and should not be sent back so soon.
He died saying the name you gave him. A Gotlander told me last summer there is no such people. I did not tell my brother. I am telling you.
Mother has the boat half loaded for the birch island. Aunt goes where there are dead to bake for. Which would you choose? I want a real answer.
I asked the twigs whether the household should go. They said the day was neither good nor bad. It is the most anyone gets.
Tell the girl: go where the ships are
Tell the girl: stay where your dead are
Lay something of your own on the mound, and say it is not yours to choose

She nods as if she had known and only wanted it said. In the spring the boat goes over with a loom's uprights, a cauldron and a crate of hens. After that somebody on Birka's jetties knows your sail at the edge of sight.
The old woman looks at you for the first time as if you were a person. The girl says nothing. The boat is unloaded again, slowly, and the farm goes on with one hearth and a long memory.
A crust and a pinch of salt, since salt is what this farm always wanted. The old woman says the dead do not mind whose it was. The girl says that was not a real answer, and that she will forgive it.
The count of the lay

The king's house. Beyond the long fire a tall stooped man with his beard in two plaits sits over a bundle of notched sticks, counting something under his breath. When he reaches the end he begins again.
A dim hall by firelight: a tall stooped man with a plaited beard holding out a notched stick across the fire to a Frisian merchant, a bundle of tally sticks at his belt, shields on the wall behind.
A Frisian. You people count coins. I count stanzas. Fifty-five in the giant's lay. I counted them this morning, and again when I saw your boat.
You are back before the ice. Good. I have a question for you, and you have, I think, six pennyweights for me.
The giant asked his guest: what is the river called that runs between the gods' land and the giants'? Six pennyweights, and you may carry it away.
You have the river's name. I see it. Say it before the bench and you drink free tonight. Say it wrong, and you drink and pay.
Your grey seaman sat a winter on this bench. The only guest who ever corrected my count. He was right. I have not told him so.
The Danes' poet at Hleidr has a stanza wrong. I have cut him my count and the stanza on a stick. It must go unread. Can you do that?
You carried it unread, and the answer back. Sit one place higher. The quarrel goes on, as it should, and it goes by your boat.
Every hall on the bay has my stanza now, each a little different. I know who carried it. Six pennyweights, as before. The seat by the door is free.
The old roof drips on the high seat. Nobody speaks of it at table. Count the hangings as you go out, and count them again in spring.
A man on a hill over the sea sends me a pelt each year, to keep me telling how his fathers took tribute there. A pelt is a pelt.
Pay six pennyweights for the giant's question
Say the river's name before the bench
Take his stick for the poet at Hleidr, unread
Listen to him count, and say nothing
He says it once, slowly, and cuts it on a stick for your chest: the question, not the answer. A lay is like a fur, he says. Count it when you get it, and count it again when you hand it on.

You say the name before the bench. He is silent for as long as it takes to count to fifty-five. Then he says the answering stanza himself, cuts it for you, and has your horn filled at the king's cost.

A hazel stick the length of a forearm, notched down one side and cut with runes on the other. He ties it with bast and seals the knot with pitch. He has counted the notches, he says. So will the Dane.
He counts to the end and begins again. Somewhere past the fortieth stanza a servant fills your cup without being asked. It seems that listening is also paid.
The answer on the back
The king's house. Vifast has seen what is in your belt from the far side of the fire. He does not get up. He holds out his hand and begins, already, to count the notches from where he sits.

Across a long fire in a timber hall: a tall stooped skald with a plaited beard holding out an open hand, a Frisian skipper drawing a notched and rune-cut stick from his belt, benches of men turning to look.
Give it here. He has cut an answer on the back. Nine notches and a stanza. I shall count it again tonight, when nobody is watching me do it.
And my side of it is in every hall on the bay. A hoarse voice at Birka, for twelve pennies' weight. I taught that voice to count.
Hand it over: carried unread, both ways
Hand it over, and say who had a look at it

He counts the notches on the answer twice and says nothing for a while. Then he moves you one place up the bench and has silver weighed out: for the carrying, he says, not for the news. The quarrel between the halls goes on, as both poets wish.

He hears who read it and nods as at a sum that has come out as expected. He pays for the carrying, less than he would have, and seats you by the door. He will go on selling to you. He will not send by you again.
A stick from the Svear
The Danes' hall at Hleidr. The king's poet takes the notched stick from you, turns it to the fire, and reads it aloud to the whole bench before you can say that it was meant for him alone.

A Danish king's hall by firelight: a poet in a good cloak holding a notched stick up to the flames and reading it aloud with one eyebrow raised, the bench laughing, a Frisian skipper standing with his hand still half out.
From Vifast. Then it is a count. Fifty-five, he says, and one stanza that I have wrong. I have it otherwise. Mine is newer, and it scans.
Did you read the front on the way? Do not tell me. A man who says no is lying or dull, and I would rather not know which.
If your grey Northman is aboard, ask him which of us is right. He will say the count is right and the stanza only older. He always does.
Wait while he cuts his answer on the back
Ask him to say the stanza his own way, aloud
He cuts for the length of two horns of ale, laughing at his own knife. Nine notches and a stanza on the back. He ties the bast again himself and says: unread. Both sides are unread now.

He says it his way, standing, to the whole bench, and it is a fine thing to hear even if it is wrong. Then he cuts his answer on the back and ties the bast. You have heard both poets now. You are not asked which was right.
The fire that is never let out

A long low house below the terrace, sledges and skis racked under the eaves. Inside, sleeping benches along both walls, a vat of ale, and a broad woman with rolled sleeves who has banked this fire every night for thirty winters.

Night in a long low guest house: a broad woman with rolled sleeves kneeling at a hearth, raking ash over red embers with an iron slice, a foreign skipper sitting up beside her, sleeping men on benches along both walls.
You have had nothing hot since Birka. Sit. Silver later; porridge first.
The Frisian. That bench, the dry end. You left a whetstone here last time. I have it.
The household is short of salt and nobody will say so at table. A man with salt would be remembered by the one who cooks.
Sit up with me tonight when I bank the fire, and I will show you some maidens. Grey ones. The skald charges for them.
You know what my maidens are. Do not tell the skald you had them for nothing. He thinks they are his.
I want a pot of the soft stone the western Northmen sell, with a lid, to keep embers alive a night and a day. Do not ask what for.
The fire on that hearth came from the old one, in your pot. Nobody thanked you aloud. That bench is yours, and your heir will be shown it.
The old hall is a red floor and nettles. I carried the fire in a kettle and burned both hands. I do not blame you. I say so twice.
The caster on the old island made the hall's cauldron chain, link by link. It is not all paid for. Tell him the hearth remembers.
Sit up with her when she banks the fire
Give the cook a sack of salt, and say nothing at table
Hand her a lidded pot of the soft stone
Eat what she gives you and sleep dry

She rakes the ash over and the red goes grey. Dust-like maidens, she says, bedded on stone: black and dull in the sun, and the less a man can see, the fairer they look. Then she tells you who has been selling them.
The sack goes behind the vat and is not mentioned. At table the porridge has salt in it for the first time in a month, and nobody says so. A bundle of bar iron is by your sea chest in the morning.

She weighs it in both hands, takes the lid off and puts it on again. On a still night after the harvest she walks out of the old hall with it, and you beside her keeping the wind off. The embers go from the old hearth to the new without going out.
Barley porridge, herring that has come a long way, and the dry end of a bench. She asks what you ate last and where, and knows from the answer how your voyage went.
No host, no peace

A low mound with its top cut level, the grass on it worn to earth by feet. A thick-set man in a fur cap sits on it with a hazel staff across his knees and a round bronze scale case on his chest, and asks his question before you have reached him.

A low flat-topped mound in trampled snow: a thick-set man in a fur cap sitting on it with a hazel staff across his knees and a folding scale held up at eye height, sledges of furs and iron drawn up behind, a foreign merchant standing below him.
A stranger with goods. Who is your host? No host, no peace. Find one, then come and I will weigh for you. Find one.
You sleep at the hearth-keeper's door. Then she answers for you, and I may weigh for you. That is the order of it.
Eight parts to the mark, three to each part. Twenty-four. If a man at Birka tells you twenty-five, bring him to me.
A Dane or a Frisian killed in this land costs less than one of us. I did not make the law. I only remember it.
The king wants ships for the summer. He has asked. The thing has not said yes. That is the order things go in here.
The trader Holmfast at Birka is my sister's son. We weigh each other's silver and are both pleased when it agrees. So far it has agreed.
A boy from Birka stands beside me at the thing and learns to argue in the rain. He will keep that town one day. Remember that I said so.
A Gotlander told me on this mound that they say their own law and ask no king's leave. I asked what it cost them. He said: nothing yet.
Say you sleep at the hearth-keeper's door, and that she answers for you
Buy a set of weights tried against his (30 d)
Buy two bundles of bar iron off the sledges, at his weighing (14 d)
Go and find a host
He hears the name and strikes the mound once with his staff. From now the thing's peace covers you as far as the boats, and a quarrel with you is a quarrel with her hearth.

He lays his own eight weights in a row and tries a new set against them, one by one, twice. They agree. With these in your purse, he says, no buyer north of the Danes can tell you what your silver weighs.

Two bundles of bar iron off a sledge from the forest country, weighed against your silver on his scale with the seller watching. He tries the silver twice. It is the cheapest iron you will see this year.
He watches you go with no ill will at all. A stranger without a host is not an enemy here. He is only nobody, until someone says otherwise.
The ninth year

Trampled snow round the flat mound, and more men than you have seen in one place north of the Rhine. It is a ninth year. For nine days the whole people is here, and the path to the old trees by the spring is roped off.
A crowd of fur-capped men seen from behind, all facing a dark stand of old trees in snow; in the foreground a lawman holding out an open scale pan to a merchant, who has a hand on his purse.
In the ninth year everyone comes, or pays. A stranger who holds another god pays sixty pennies' weight. Not small, and not ruinous. I did not set it.
Your men have split. The old hands say a man should see a thing before he judges it. The baptised will not go near the trees.
Every Svea with a skin to sell is here. Whoever stays away loses the best market of nine years. That is not the law. It is only true.
You weighed out the fine the last time and kept the law. It was noticed, by both kinds of people.
Weigh out the fine, and keep to the guest house for nine days
Go with the people, and stand where a guest stands
Take your goods down the river until the moon after
The silver goes into the pan and he tries it twice. Nobody thinks the worse of you: it is the law, and you kept it. Nine days is a long time to hear a feast through a wall.

You are a guest of the whole people for nine days and eat at the king's cost. What you saw you do not tell your crew, and the baptised among them do not ask. Every sledge at the market is open to you.
No fine and no feast. You lose the best market of nine years and go down the river past men still coming up it. The lawman notes who was absent, as he notes everything, without heat.
A hand too much water

A low clay bank where the grey river widens for the last time: a dozen small boats among willows, a sledge on its side, three round hills on the skyline that are not hills. A lean wind-brown man with a coiled net on his shoulder is looking at your waterline, not at you.

A low clay river bank among willows with a dozen small boats drawn up: a lean wind-brown man in a hooded grey cloak, a coiled net on one shoulder and a brace of duck on the other, pointing at a boat's waterline; flat wet meadow and three round mounds on the skyline.
Your boat draws a hand too much for the upper reach. Leave her here. The cranes left here too, this morning.
The water is down two fingers since you came last. Same place. I kept the willow clear for you.
Merry maids glide over the land, to their father's joy. In winter they carry a white shield, in summer a black. I made that. Somebody made it before me.
When the teal go south before the birch turns, the bay shuts early. They went six days ago.
Two sledges of marten came down last night and passed the market by. Somebody at Birka has paid. I trap for a man in the east. He pays late.
My mother's kinsman takes ships through the sounds below Birka. Between us we know the water from the sea to the mounds. He has the deep end.
You took me down the river and brought me back. So: this month she floats as far as the second willow, no further. Ask each time. It changes.
Give him passage down to Birka and back
Tell him what his maids are
Buy a brace of duck and a sack of down (5 d)
Leave the boat where he says

He sits in the bow the whole way down and names every bird. At Birka he looks at the town for one evening and asks to go home. He gives you his riddle to carry, and promises you the river to the hand's breadth when he is back.
You tell him. He looks at the sky as if it had been listening, and gives you a sack of down he had been keeping for somebody else.
Two fat mallard and a sack of down. He will not haggle. The price of a duck is what it was when the water was deeper, he says, and it is the only thing here that has not changed.
You leave her among the willows where he points. When you come back down she has been bailed, and there is a feather stuck in the stem. He does not say what for.
Forty threads to the thumb

Thirty small roofs that seem to sit on the ground, each over a pit a man can stand in. Through one door a row of clay weights swings on a loom as tall as the roof, and a slight woman measures cloth along her arm and says a number twice.

Seen down through the low door of a sunken house: a tall upright loom with a row of clay weights swinging, a slight woman in a blue strap dress with a bone weaving-sword, lint in the air, a merchant on the threshold holding out a bolt of cloth.
Frisian cloth? Let me feel it. Do not tell me where it is from. I will tell you.
Forty threads to the thumb, your last bolt. I counted. Forty. Bring that again and I will find iron for it.
The household pays me in what it has. Bring madder, and I will pay you in what I have: wadmal that keeps out the sea.
That is Ragnvi's thumb in the pitch. Unopened. Good. Most boats cannot manage it.
They took the good hangings out of the hall last week. All of them. Nobody takes hangings down for a feast.
The man next door is curling bar iron into spirals, like fern heads, and wants more iron than the estate has. Ask him what for. He will not say.
The fowler brings me down that I have not asked for. I have noticed. I have not said so. Do not you say so.
Give her the bead-maker's bundle, unopened
Take her order for madder
Trade a bolt of Frisian cloth for iron and wadmal
Watch the weaving-sword go, and leave her to it

She looks at the thumbprint before she looks at you. Then she cuts the stitches, counts the beads on to her apron, and counts them again. Two bolts of wadmal for the carrying, and she says your boat may carry for her again.
Two sacks of the red root, by this time next year. She will pay half again what it costs on your river, in iron or cloth and not in silver. She says the count twice, once to you and once to herself.
She runs the bolt through her fingers with her eyes shut and tells you which river the wool grew by. She is right. Three bundles of bar iron and three bolts of wadmal are found for it before evening.
The weaving-sword goes up and the weights knock together. She has said her count for the row before you are out of the door, and said it again.
Delling's door

The king's house below the burnt terrace. A small quick man with a rune stick behind one ear like a carpenter's wedge is laughing at something, and then counting on his fingers whether it was worth laughing at.
Five rune sticks laid in a fan on a ship's thwart, a folding scale beside them, and beyond the gunwale a low grey island under a pale sun with a darker patch of cloud close behind it.
A Frisian house. Wait. My mother's grandfather notched a Frisian. Here: one boat, four men, pays in good silver, corrects nobody. Is that you?
You again, and dry. I have never understood how you people do it.
The High One asked the giant: where does the day come from, and the night with her moon? Eight pennyweights, and a door to stand before.
You have the father of day. His door comes next, and what stands before it. A Gotland skald has that stick, on the beach where they mend boats.
Three doors opened and the fourth answered. Then the last stick is yours to find, not mine to sell. Walk up the middle mound with me at sunrise.
I was in a boat off Gotland once, and have made verses about staying ashore since. Go round the sea for me. I shall be here. I always am.
Weights go by the eastern coin now. The lawman's set is true. The set at Birka is true on market days.
I made a verse of it in which I sail round the sea myself. The king laughed and asked who truly went. To my credit, I pointed.
Pay eight pennyweights for the first stick
Walk up the middle mound with him at sunrise
Give him the five answers, and say the floor on Gotland stays down
Hear his verse about your boat

He takes the stick from behind his ear, finds it is the wrong one, and fetches another. The first of five, he says. The others are a long way off, and the last cannot be bought. He has never seen the end of it himself.

Nobody stands on the middle mound to talk business; he does it out of breath and before the sun is clear. He tells you what his mother's grandfather notched last: who it is that fells the father of men. The answer, he says, names a farm.

He counts the five answers on his fingers and laughs first, then counts again whether it was worth it. It was. The king hears, and five hundred pennies' weight in rings comes down the bench from a hand you never quite see.
It rhymes with nothing, like the sea, and it has your boat in it, low in the water and dry inside. He says praise is safest from the shore.
The England-farer's stone

A tall red-grey boulder lies on trestles in the grave field, and a carver is chipping a snake of runes along it. A big man in a red English cloak tips a purse of pennies onto the cloak's corner and looks up as if you had been sent for.

A tall red-grey boulder lying on trestles in a grave field, a carver chipping a snake of runes along it, a big man in a red English cloak watching, a merchant beside him holding a penny up to the light.
You are from the south. Good. Look at this penny and tell me the king's name on it. I know it. I want to hear you say it.
The Frisian! I told my wife about the river at London again. She says it has grown since Yule.
They pay you to go away, the English. Then another fleet comes, and they pay that one. I have never seen a people so rich or so tired.
The king here is baptised, and the feast here is kept. I wear both. A man should not be poorer in gods than in silver.
I left London owing forty pennies at a moneyer's bench. I have meant to send it for ten years. A stone should not go up over a debt.
A third of my bag was light. I said the English had cheated me. Then I said I had rather know. I say that still, most days.
Sort his pennies truly, good from light, for a fair share
Tell him the good ones are light, and buy them cheap
Stand by the carver and say whether his father's name is cut right
Say the king's name on the penny, and go

You sort them on the cloak: the king's head and true to the right, the light ones to the left. A third of the bag goes left. He is silent, then pays the carver from the right-hand heap and gives you your share from it too.

You call the good ones light and take them off his hands at a light price. A hundred and eighty pennies in an afternoon. At the new town the moneyer will weigh what he has left and tell him what he had. He will not use your name again.
You follow the snake with a finger: Sigvid, the England-farer, raised this stone for Vedjarf, his father. The carver has spelled it right. Sigvid lets out a breath he has been holding since London.
You say the name on the penny. He nods as if you had passed something, puts the penny back in the bag and tells you about the river at London. It is very wide.
Where a bishop may stand

The king's new town on the lake: one long street of gravel, plots running down to the water like the teeth of a comb. By a small wooden church a spare, tonsured man with a book satchel is being told, politely, by two of the king's men, how far up the river he may go.

A gravel street along a lake shore with narrow plots running down to the water: a spare tonsured man in a dark travelling cloak over a white alb, a book satchel at his side, standing before a small wooden church while two armed men point up the lake.
A Christian from the Rhine mouth. God sent you, or the wind did. Have you room in your boat for a chest of books, going either way?
You come and go freely. I am told where I may stand. Tell me what they say of me at Uppsalir.
I asked the king for leave to burn it. He said they would kill me and cast him out. He said it kindly.
In a ninth year a Christian here pays silver to stay away from the feast. They call it a fine. I call it the cheapest thing they sell.
You carry writing. I can see the shape of the case. Show me. I have read every leaf I own until I can see through it.
Show him a leaf from your chest
Hear his Mass at first light before you sail
Tell him what they say of him up the river
Greet him and go about your trade

He reads it standing in the street, aloud, slowly, and then explains it to you, which takes longer. You understand more of the letters than you did. He hands it back as a hungry man hands back a dish.
A dozen people in a wooden church at first light, and a bishop who says the whole of it as if there were a thousand. He names those who sail. He does not ask their names first.

You tell him: that he is a learned man who wants one fire, and that the king likes him and will not have it. He says the apostle did not ask leave of the Ephesians. Then he says the apostle was not the king's guest.
He blesses the boat from the shore without being asked. One of the king's men watches him do it and then watches you, and says nothing to either.
Under the boat hill

Half an hour upriver of the estate, a steep grass hill with long low hollows in its side, each the length of a boat. Under it, by the water, two open sheds, a steaming trough and a slim boat in frame. The wrights do not look at the hill while they work.

A steep grass hill with long boat-shaped hollows in its side, and under it by a river two open sheds, a steaming trough, split oak stacked to season and a slim clinker boat in frame, a wright with an adze looking down at a small southern boat.
You came up from the estate to look at a boat in frame. Look. She is for the river and the bay. Your sea would break her.
The Frisian. She is planked now, as you see. The next will be for a man who is not yet dead, which makes a change.
The hollows in the hill are boats. One man to a boat, with shield and dogs. We do not look up while we work. They do not look down.
She wants a sail. Our women weave for backs, not for wind. Bring me a bolt of sailcloth by next thaw and I pay half again its price.
A bolt of sailcloth, by the thaw. I have cut it on the stem post, where I shall see it every morning until you come.
Take his order for a bolt of sailcloth
Buy a barrel of tar at the shed (14 d)
Have him knock along your own boat's strakes (2 d)
Look at the boat in frame, and at the hill

He cuts a notch on the stem post of the boat in frame: one bolt, by the thaw. Half again its price, in bar iron or in silver as you choose. The last man who promised him cloth is in the hill, he says, though not for that.

A barrel of pine tar from the pits upriver, black and thin, knocked shut with a mallet. Fourteen pennies' weight. On your own river it fetches half as much again, and he knows it. He says the river is long.
He walks round your boat once, knocking, and stops twice. Here and here, he says, before the autumn. He takes two pennies' weight for it, and tells you nothing that you did not fear already.

A slim hull in frame, clean oak, the strakes thin as the edge of a hand. Above the sheds the long hollows lie in the grass, each the length of a boat. The wrights do not look up, and after a while neither do you.
The row of posts

A trodden way of brushwood and planks runs north across flooded grass. Beside it a line of great grey posts marches off towards the mounds, some upright and taller than a mast, many leaning, more only stumps. Cranes stand in the shallows. Your bales are on the bank, and the estate is at the far end of the planks.

A plank and brushwood way running across flooded grass under a wide sky: a line of great grey posts marching toward three distant mounds, some leaning, some only stumps, cranes in the shallows, a lean man with a fowling net beside a sledge loaded with bales.
Keep to the brushwood. Off it you are in to the knee, and your bale to the cord. Six men and a sledge cost three pennies' weight.
The posts? Older than the mounds, some say, and some say younger. They go to the mounds in a line. Nobody sets one up again when it falls.
The cranes are in. When they stand in the shallows like that, the plain will not dry this month. I take the first of them to the hearth-keeper.
In late summer they lead stallions out here and set them at each other, and men lay silver on it. I lay mine on the cranes. They come back.
Hire six men and a sledge across the plain (3 d)
Have your own men carry the bales
Ask him what the posts are for
Six men and a sledge with runners of ash. They do not speak to you, and they do not drop a bale. At the far end one of them holds out a hand, and tests the three pennies' weight with his teeth.
Your own men carry it, two to a bale, and one goes in to the thigh at the place the fowler pointed out. Everything arrives. Nobody sings on the way back.

He tells it the way he tells where the pike lie. A line of posts, from before his grandfather, going to the mounds. Fires were lit at their feet once; you can see the black. What for, he says, is a question for the skald, who will charge you.
The gift at the door

A long curve of pale shingle on still brown water, boats on rollers, square sails spread to dry in chequers of two colours. A straight-backed woman with keys at her belt has walked down from the farm, and waits where the shingle ends.

A long curve of pale shingle on still brown water: clinker boats on rollers with chequered sails spread to dry, a straight-backed woman of fifty with keys at her belt and round box brooches on a brown dress standing where the shingle ends, a small Frisian boat just grounded, low sheds and thin smoke behind.
You are on my shore. That is no complaint. Bring something to the door, eat what you are given, and you are my guest and not a stranger.
The same boat, and the same man with the big laugh in it. He sleeps at the far end this time. You are welcome. Come and eat.
Last time you brought the gift to the door yourself, not by a boy. It was noticed. Same gift this time. I do not raise it for friends.
A stranger's life is ten marks here, and one of ours twenty-four. I did not make the sum. Stay near my fire and nobody has to do it.
There is no toll man. People come from the Franks' rivers and look round for one as if they had lost a dog.
They say this island sank under the sea every morning, until a man carried fire onto it. I have a nephew like that. He needs watching by day.
A weaver's house at Birka lodges my kin, and I lodge hers. Each sends the other the cloth and cheese she thinks better. Nobody is winning.
A north-shore woman asks every boat from the Este's lake after her man. He went up a river with blades. You look like one who counted his silver.
A floor was lifted in the north-east while the farmer was at sea. I do not say by whom. Haul your own boat up today. My nephews are busy.
A farmer in the north-east has spoken for your house at the ring. I do not ask why. You sit above my nephews tonight.
The people you set down on this beach from the Cori's shore have a roof on the north side now. They name your boat when they pour.
Carry a sack of salt up to her door yourself
Send a boy up with four pennies' weight of silver
Give her the purse from under the post at the lake of the Este
Sleep aboard, and bring nothing

You carry it up yourself and set it inside the door. She weighs it with her eyes, pretends to be insulted that it is salt, and has a bowl in your hands before you have straightened up. Your men sleep in the shelter under her farm's word.
The boy comes back with a nod and half a loaf. It is enough: you may lie on the shore and sleep in the shelter. It is also remembered that you sent a boy.

Eleven whole and five cut. She has the woman fetched from the north shore, and it is weighed before both farms and found exact. The thick old coin with the crowned head they give back to you: it brought him no luck, and may suit a Frisian better.
Nobody stops you. Nobody brings fish broth down to the boat either, and in the morning the place on the rollers you had your eye on belongs to someone who brought a gift.
The weight, not the name

The strip of trodden ground where the stream meets the lagoon. No booths: hides spread on the stones, and every second man holding a small folding balance up against the light off the water. You have offered pennies by count, and the seller has called the smith.

The weighing shore in low evening light: a lean smith with burnt forearms holding a small folding balance up against the water, one Frankish penny in the pan, a foreign merchant watching the beam, beads and combs spread on a hide between them.
Put your silver on the pan, not in my hand. I do not know your king. I know what he weighs.
The Frisian with the heavy pennies. Good silver, your king's. A pity he spoils it with his name. What did you bring me that is not silver?
You pay by count. Then you are paid by the lightest penny in your bag, here and on every beach where there is no king. I can cure that.
You carry a balance. Whose pouring? Let me try one weight against my father's. Good. Somebody honest taught you.
A skipper home from the east paid me half a coin last autumn. White, with writing round it like ants. Better silver than yours, and no king on it.
The bright cubes come from the south, out of old walls. Some have gold shut in the glass. I melt them. A bead is seen oftener than a wall.
The amber is poor this year. The Este are keeping the big pieces for somebody. Ask at their lake who it is, and tell me.
