The last caster on the Svear's holy island and I compared weights half a day. His are true, and he has no metal. Mine are true, and I have.
Pay him to pour you weights and teach the beam (26 d)
Pay for the lesson with a sack of raw glass
Give him a sack of raw glass for three strings of beads
Say a penny is a penny, and pay by count

He nicks a penny, bends it on his thumbnail and rings it on a stone, and makes you do each after him. Then he pours eight weights and shows you the beam. You leave with a folding balance in a bronze case. On the next beach nobody calls a smith.

He turns the cubes over in the light for a long time before he says anything. Then he pours your weights from his own bronze and files each one against his father's set, which he has not done for a stranger before.
You tip the sack onto his clay platform. He sorts the cubes by colour without speaking, the gold ones last, and counts out three strings of beads from the first rod of the summer.

They take your pennies, each one weighed against the lightest in the bag. You are not cheated. You are simply paid what the worst of them is worth, as you will be on every beach where there is no king.
Let me knock on her first

A hull lies on the shingle with half her planks on, pale new wood over dark. A broad man in a leather apron black with tar sights along her with one eye shut, and has not yet decided whether to notice you.

A shingle slip beside a still lagoon: a half-planked hull with rows of rivet heads, a broad short-legged man in a tarred leather apron with wood chips in his beard rapping his knuckles on the strakes of a small Frisian boat, an adze laid down on a block.
A Frisian boat. Short in the keel and full in the bow. Who built her? No, do not tell me. Let me knock on her first.
She came back, then. I looked at her from the shed when you rounded the point. The third strake on the steering side is weeping.
Who is the big one that wades in the deep, half turned toward the dead? He saves men, and pulls against the ground. Three pennies' weight, on a stick.
You have it. Your old Northman had it before I had finished saying it. I have not forgiven him, and I like him for it.
A Dane learned his trade on this slip and went home to Skane. He sends word when he wants rivets. He never sends word that I was right.
The lagoon is a hand shallower than when my father hauled boats here. Nobody believes me. The boats believe me.
Holmfast of Birka had his ship planked here and counted her rivets afterwards. He still owes me the last ounce. He says he is weighing it.
A stone with two birds, for a woman over the sea? I cut wood. The stone-cutter is up the slope, among his customers. I think she is my kin.
Buy his riddle, cut on a stick (3 d)
Tell him what the big one is
Have him set the weeping strake right (10 d)
Let him knock on her, and listen
He cuts it while you wait and hands it over without a word about what it says. He sells this to every skipper, and he has been right about most of their boats.
You say it. He puts down his adze, which with him is either very good or very bad, and walks round your boat knocking on every strake for nothing.
Out comes a hand's length of soft plank and in goes a piece of seasoned pine, with four new rivets clenched over roves. She will tell you when she needs him again, he says, and you are to listen.
He knocks along her from stem to stern with one knuckle and his head on one side. Sound, he says. Sound. Not that one. Sound. He tells you which, and that it will keep until autumn.
Ten feet, three eyes, one tail

A slope of short grass and juniper south of the hearths, set with low rings and heaps of stone. A thin grey man with stone dust in his beard kneels at a slab of limestone lying flat, tapping a pointed iron along a line only he can see.

A grassy slope of low stone settings above a lagoon: a thin grey man with sheepskin-wrapped knees kneeling at a flat limestone slab with mallet and pointed iron, a tall painted picture stone with a ship under a chequered sail behind him, a merchant crouching to look.
A living man. They are rarer up here than you would think. Mind the slab; it is somebody's father.
You again, and still alive. I had half a mind to start on your ship. What does she carry at the stern, so that I get it right?
Who are the two that have ten feet, three eyes and one tail? I cut them on every second stone. Nobody who pays for a stone ever asks.
Ten feet, three eyes, one tail. You have it. The horse has eight legs because it is fast, or because four men carry a bier. I was told both.
Two birds, facing? Nobody has asked for birds since my grandfather's day. I cut ships and riders. But you have a drawing. I can cut what is drawn.
It is cut, and wrapped in a fleece. Two water birds. I do not know which either. Carry it gently over that bar. I shall never make another.
A woman ordered a stone for a son who went east. No body. I cut the ship a little smaller when there is no body. Nobody has noticed.
Tell me how the Franks mark their dead. If it is a heap of stones with a stick on it, I do not want to know.
Ask him what the pictures on the stones mean
Say who the two are
Give him the drawing and the widow's silver for a stone with two birds (40 d)
Sit on the grass and watch him cut

He gives you a question in place of an answer, and a stanza cut on a stick besides, for nothing. A thing explained is a thing spoiled, he says. The woman with the horn is welcoming somebody. He will not say who.
You say who the two are. He looks at you with stone dust in his eyebrows and says the dead on this slope are better company than most of the living, but that you may come up whenever you like.

He lays the birch bark on a slab the length of a child and marks through it with the iron. Two birds, facing, the size they are on the old stone over the sea. Forty pennies' weight, and he asks for the bark as well, to keep.
Tap, and tap, and the line of a sail comes out of the stone a finger at a time. He speaks of the man under it as if he were expected back this evening.
An evening in the shelter

A long low shelter above the shore: posts, a roof of turf and reed, a floor of beaten gravel, the fourth side open to the water. Men sit on their sea chests round a fire with a board of pegged pieces between them, and somebody is mending a net.

The open end of a reed-roofed shelter at evening: men sitting on sea chests round a fire with a pegged gaming board between two of them, a long loose-limbed skipper with a silver ring high on his arm, a farmer with a cup, a net being mended, the lagoon bright behind.
A boat from the Rhine mouth on this beach. You are either lost or clever. Sit down and tell me which.
The Frisian. Good. I told my wife you would come back, and she said no man sails that far twice for beads.
There is a town on a river in the east where a sword buys more furs than the boat will hold. I am not telling you which river.
Two boats from the north of the island are not home, and the nights are drawing in. Nobody says anything yet. We do not say it until the frost.
I saw a household merry at sundown in summer. The men drank in silence, and the ale-cask stood up and screamed. A townsman will not get it.
My kin keep booths on the Cori's shore, under the hornbeam fort. I sleep at old Botgair's fire going east. He weighs fair, and is thought a fool.
The Svea Holmfast weighed my wax three times at Birka. I asked whether it had grown. He weighed it again.
Take the farmer's riddle away with you
Tell the farmer what stood up and screamed
Ask the skipper what the east pays for
Splice rope by their fire and say little
The farmer says it again, slower, as to a child, and laughs into his cup. You carry it off. He farms forty sheep and a great many pigs, and that is all the help he gives.
You tell him. He is put out, then delighted, and says a townsman who knows that has stood in a sty at least once. You sleep at his farm that night, not in the shelter.
He answers a question about silver with a question about the weather. Then, later, by the fire: blades, glass and good cloth. If you want to talk about it, he says, the place is not his door.
You splice a rope's end and listen to an argument about a move on the board that happened three winters ago. Nobody asks what you carry. On this beach that is a courtesy.
A hand on the stone

In the middle of the working ground, with hearths on every side of it, stands a ring of grey stones as wide as a boat is long, the grass inside it uncut. The skipper has walked you here instead of to his door, which on this island means business.

A ring of grey stones among smoking hearths at dusk, the grass inside uncut: a long loose-limbed skipper with one hand flat on the nearest stone, a Frisian merchant facing him with a purse, low light off the lagoon throwing the stones' shadows as far as the yard wall.
I go east at the next fair wind, with room to spare. Put something in my hold. Shares by what each puts in. The reckoning before the frost.
We swear it here, each with a hand on the stone. No stick is cut. A thing sworn at the ring is known to everybody by evening.
I have been lucky nine summers. I do not say ten. Nobody on this beach says ten.
Swear, and put sixty pennies' weight into his hold
Swear, and put two bare blades into his hold
Say you put silver only where you can see it

A hand each on the cold stone, and the words said once. He weighs your silver on his own scale and then, because you are a stranger, on the smith's. By evening the whole beach knows a Frisian has a share in his hold.
He bends each blade over his knee behind the yard wall, where nobody can see, and lets it spring. Then a hand each on the stone. He knows a man on a river, he says, who will smile when he sees them.
He shrugs and says it is how a man stays small and dry. He does not hold it against you. He asks about the weather on the way back to the shelter, and means it this time.
Home, and low in the water

The dragging beach, and one boat more on the rollers than when you left. She sat low when she came in; the whole shore saw it and nobody has said a word. The skipper is waiting by her stem with his scale case in his hand.

A shingle beach in autumn light: a broad sea-stained boat just hauled onto rollers, bundles of dark furs and yellow cakes of wax being handed down, a long loose-limbed skipper holding up a folding scale, neighbours watching from the sheds without seeming to.
I am home, and she was low. Before the frost, as I said. We weigh it on your scale and mine, and then my neighbour's. He is watching anyway.
Your two blades bought more than the rest of my hold together. I have seen it weighed. I have seen the man smile who paid.
Ten summers now. I did not say it. You said it.
Take your share in marten and wax
Take your share in the white silver, by weight
Take what your two blades bought

A timber of marten, forty skins counted twice, and a cake of wax the size of a quern. On the Rhine that is nearly three times what you put on the stone. He asks whether you will swear again next spring.

Thin white coins with writing all round, whole and cut, weighed out to a hundred and thirty pennies' weight. He does not say where the rest of his own share will sleep tonight. Under a floor, you suppose.
Three timbers of dark marten for two bare blades. The man on the river asked whether the Frisian had brothers, he says. He told him you had a king who would not like it.
Before Delling's door

The open end of the shelter at dusk. An old man with a rune-cut stick across his knees is asking one question of whoever sits on the benches, as he does every evening, and the lagoon is going dark behind him.

The open end of a reed-roofed shelter at dusk: an old man with a rune-cut stick across his knees, firelight on his face, a ring of seated crewmen and a merchant leaning forward, the lagoon dark behind them and the first stars out.
Each evening I ask one, and nobody on this beach answers. Sit. Tonight's is as old as I am, and I did not make it.
This stick is not for one who has not stood before the door. Go up the Svear's river and pay their poet first. He is afraid of boats.
You have the father of day. Then this is owed you. What did I see before Delling's door? Its head turns to the dead, its feet to the sun.
The next is in the eastern river town. A host there keeps it for a week's ale never paid. Say the Gotlander sent you, and pay your own.
The stick lay under a keel some winters, as a charm against rot. The boat did not rot. The wright wants it back. I say: good tar.
Every Gotlander will tell you a farmer in the north-east sleeps on more silver than a king eats off. Every Gotlander will tell you it is another farmer.
Say the father of day, and take the second stick
Tell him what stood before the door
Listen to tonight's question with the rest
He puts the stick in your hand: old, dark with tar on one side, the runes worn soft. The answer is not on this island, he says, though it grows in every garden on it.
You tell him. He grunts, which from him is applause, and says the thing has stood before that door since before the Svear had kings, with its head in the ground.
Tonight's question is about something with no feet that outruns a horse. Nobody answers. He seems content. He will ask another tomorrow, of whoever is here.
A new floor

Two days round the north of the island in a borrowed boat, with the skald's boy to point the way. A bay, a ship drawn up, and above it a farm of grey stone and turf. The farmer has come to his door. Behind him the floor of the house is new: flat slabs, tight-laid, swept.

A grey stone farmhouse above a bay on a bare coast: a broad farmer in the doorway with his thumbs in his belt, a new floor of flat swept slabs seen past him, a trading ship drawn up on the shore below, a boy waiting in a small boat.
You have come a long way round to look at a farm. Sit. A guest gets ale before he is asked his business. After that he is asked.
The Frisian who looks at floors. You drank my ale and said nothing last time. I have thought about that since. Sit.
I laid it the year the boats came home full. A man should have a floor under him that he can trust. This one I trust.
My ship goes east with the next fair wind, and I go in her. My wife's people keep the farm. They sleep soundly. I chose them for it.
The skald's boy has not come up from the boat. He said the questions were his master's business, and the farm was nobody's.
Tell him what five sticks say about his floor
Say nothing, and come back with a spade when his sail is gone
Drink his ale, praise the floor, and go

He listens without moving. Then he goes out, and comes back with arm-rings on a cord, the weight of twelve hundred pennies, and lays them by your cup. He asks who else has the sticks, and you tell him. Within the year two of them will be in his chest, and the silver stays where it is.

Three nights later the bay is empty and the farm asleep. The slabs come up easily; they were laid to. There is more under them than your boat should carry, and more than you can spend unseen. You mark what you can lift before the dogs wake. You will not land on this island again.
It is good ale. He walks you down to the bay himself and stands there until your boat is round the point. The skald's boy says nothing all the way home, and you are both content with that.
One stone, two shapes

A small house with walls of piled limestone and no hearth, cold inside on the hottest day. On a ledge lies a block of yellow sandstone with one shape cut into it: a short stem and two arms. The smith tips a bright thing out of it into his palm.

Inside a cold stone-walled store by lamplight: a smith holding a block of yellow sandstone with a T-shaped hollow cut in it, a newly cast silver pendant on his palm, an old farmer with a hammer amulet at his neck and a young skipper with a cross at his, both watching.
Hung stem down, it is a hammer. Stem up, a cross. I sell more this way up than I did. Which it is, nobody has paid me to decide.
Hammer or cross, it is half an ounce of silver, and I weigh it the same.
They poured water on me in England. I want a priest brought to this island, quietly. The Danes' west market has one to spare. Has your boat room?
A wooden house for the new god was burnt on this island not long ago. The old farmers say it was a pity about the timber.
He says his Mass in a barn on my farm. Some come. Nobody has burnt the barn. The old farmers were cool for a year. Then wool went up.
Buy a pair of them, and say it is not your stone (20 d)
Carry the young skipper west to fetch his priest
Say a Frisian boat carries cargo, not quarrels
He pours two while you wait and weighs them on one pan. You hang neither. Your crew wear what they like under their shirts, as they always have.

He comes aboard with a sea chest and thirty pennies for the passage, and looks back at the island only once. If the priest is willing he will bring him home in some other hull, quietly, by the outlet quays.
The young skipper shrugs and says there are other boats. The smith says nothing. Next morning there is a cheese on your thwart, and no word with it, from one of the old farms.
Rivets by the hundred

South of the yard the ground is laid with flat stones, black with soot between them. Three hearths, a stump with an iron block set in it, and two men drawing rivets by the hundred and throwing them hissing into a trough. It smells of hot iron and singed horn.

A working floor of flat soot-black stones with three hearths, one under a turf roof on posts: two men at a stump with an iron block, drawing rivets and throwing them into a steaming trough, scraps of bronze and bent iron lying where they fell.
A hundred to the string, and every one of them will hold a strake. We draw them all winter and they are gone by midsummer. Boats eat iron.
Is that bar iron under your thwart? Svea iron is best, yours is second, and second is what I can get. Put it on the stone.
Three boats are fitting for the east, and each wants four strings before she will float. Come back in autumn if you want me idle.
Buy a string of a hundred rivets (12 d)
Sell him a bundle of bar iron (14 d)
Have your own loose rivets knocked tight (3 d)
Stand out of the sparks, and watch

A string of a hundred, still warm, each with its square rove. He bites the knot off and hands it over. They will hold a strake on any hull between here and the Rhine, he says, and he has never seen the Rhine.

He strikes the bar once on the iron block and listens to it. Fourteen pennies' weight, in cut silver, weighed twice. The island has stone, sheep and seamen, he says. Iron it has to buy, and so it has learned to count.

Two men go along your boat with a hammer and a holding-iron, and knock at every rove from stem to stern. Nine are loose. They draw them tight without comment. The boat sounds different afterwards when the sea slaps her.

A rod is heated, cut, headed and thrown hissing into the trough, and then again, and the hammers never keep the same time. One of the men grins at you through the smoke. It is honest work, and there is no end to it.
What the king's head weighs

A trodden space between the shore and the first plots, with no stalls. Men stand in pairs, one holding a little folding scale up to the light, the other watching the pans. A broad Dane with grey in his plaited beard has your purse open on his palm.

A folding scale held up against a grey lake: in one pan three Frankish pennies with a king's monogram, in the other half a dirham and a nugget of amber; a broad Dane's hand holding the beam, a Frisian's face behind it, doubtful.
A Frisian boat, and small. You came the whole way in that? Then you can count, or you are lucky. Sit. I will find out which.
The same boat. I told the fort a Frisian would be back with the open water. They said strangers do not come twice. Mead?
Your king's head is very fine. Put it in the pan. Here the king's head weighs what the king's head weighs.
The new heavy ones do well. These thin old ones I hand back with one finger. Is this the first place your purse was worth less than its count?
Look. A penny of yours. Half a coin with writing like worm tracks. A thick one, with a crowned head nobody can name. All good. Only one needs explaining.
The goldsmith will sell you a scale. He cannot sell you the knowing. That is three evenings at my bench, cutting and weighing, until your pieces come even.
Do not look for one king to complain to. Every fort in this land has its own, and no two of them are friends.
A man from the fort asked me what a penny is. I said: silver a king has spoken to. He asked whether it weighs more afterwards.
A goldsmith on the Danes' river in Skane has weights off my mould. We tried them once. Tell him Ketil's still agree. He will pretend to doubt it.
You passed thin pennies by count on the low bench. Nameda knew by evening. I weigh for both sides and say nothing. She is not obliged to.
Let him nick all three silvers, and hold them
Buy the goldsmith's scale, and sit three evenings at his bench (30 d)
Pass your thin old pennies by count to a gatherer from the low bench
Keep to your king's penny, and sell here only for goods

He nicks each with his knife and lays them on your palm: a penny, half a coin of the caliphs, and a thick old king of nowhere. They weigh as silver and nothing more. A Svea gave him the old one for luck, he says, and it has not yet done anything.

Three evenings of cutting silver and weighing the pieces until they come out even. On the third he lets you weigh for a Gotlander, and does not check. The scale goes into your chest in its round bronze case.
It works once, on a gatherer from the low bench who cannot weigh. You are six pennies to the good. Ketil saw, and looks at the lake. By evening the whole shore will have heard it from somebody else.
You never lose a grain to a strange coin here, and never gain one. Cloth for marten, iron for amber, at a fair rate. Ketil says it is a respectable way to stay small.
Three heaps on a cloth

A low shore of grey shingle and trodden reed, boats drawn up side by side with their sterns in brown still water. A sunburnt woman kneels at a cloth spread with three heaps of wet yellow lumps, a forked rake beside her, and has seen your purse before you have seen her.

A low reedy shore with boats drawn up: a sunburnt woman with bronze spirals sewn to her apron kneeling at a cloth with three heaps of wet yellow lumps, a forked rake beside her, a Frisian rubbing one piece on his sleeve, a broad Dane with scales looking carefully at the lake.
Sea-stone. West shore, after the storm. All good. You have honest eyes: I will take your silver gently.
The Frisian who rubs every piece on his sleeve. Sit. Today I have nothing false. Nearly nothing.
Thin pennies on the low bench. I heard by evening. Today every heap I show you has resin in it. Bring cloth, and my eyes will get better.
North gale, three nights at the dark of the moon. We stood in the water to the waist with nets. The sheds are full. Do not tell the Dane.
Sleeve, brine, lip. You know them now. I sort my heaps more carefully when I see your sail, which is a great nuisance.
The best I ever raked had a fly in it, legs and all. The fort took it. A fly, and they call me a cheat.
A Frisian at the Wends' market cuts my stone into beads and pays a season behind. Tell him the sea gives no credit. I do, a little.
Buy a sack from the middle heap, by eye (22 d)
Rub, float and taste, and buy a sack of true stone (22 d)
Give her a bolt of woollen cloth for her daughters' cloaks
Buy nothing, and ask to be shown how she tells true stone
You pick by eye from the middle heap, and she weighs it with a face like a shut door. It is true stone, every piece. She says she liked you better before you were lucky.

Half the sack is boiled resin and two pieces are yellow glass. She laughs at the end, hands you a bowl of brine and shows you which swim. You are twenty-two pennies' weight poorer, and cannot be cheated this way again.
You rub each piece on your sleeve, float it and put it to your lip. She watches you lay four back on her cloth and says nothing. The sack you carry off is sea-stone to the last lump.
She feels the weave, bites the edge and calls her daughters. A sack of sorted stone comes out of the shed for it, and she thinks she has robbed you. So do you. It is the only honest trade.
Sleeve: it pulls chaff. Brine: it swims. Lip: it is warm. Glass is cold, and resin stinks. Now you know, she says, and she is the poorer.
Amber for the count's lady

Small houses with their doors propped open to the south for the light, strings of beads turning in the wind. You owe the count of Dorestad an errand in place of silver, and his steward said what the lady wants: sea-stone from the far shore, clear, and matched.

A row of small houses with doors propped open to the sun: strings of amber beads turning in the wind on a door post, a sunburnt woman holding up one matched string against the light, a Frisian merchant weighing it in his palm, honey-coloured chips on the threshold.
For a great man's wife? Not from the heap. From the bowl. These swim in brine and are warm on the lip. Clear as honey, each like the next.
The cutter on this row drills them and I match them. Sixty pennies' weight the string. Or cloth. I would rather have cloth.
A king far off once sent word to tell us what this is. We were glad to know. We had only been picking it up.
And you are the one with the thin pennies. For this I weigh your silver myself, twice. Or bring cloth, and we are friends.
Buy a matched string of clear stone, cut and drilled (60 d)
Give two bolts of Frisian cloth for the matched string
Buy a sack of raw stone and let the count find a cutter (24 d)
Look, and buy nothing yet
Twenty-one beads, clear as honey, each the twin of the next, on a thread of flax. She wraps the string in a scrap of fleece. It weighs almost nothing, and is the dearest thing in your boat.
Two bolts of Frisian blue for a string of beads. She is certain she has robbed you. The string goes into your chest in a scrap of fleece, and the thin pennies are not mentioned again.
A sack of raw lumps, honest sea-stone, uncut. It will do, if somebody on the Rhine can cut it and the lady can wait. Great men's wives are not known for waiting.
You look. The strings turn in the wind. She says the first boat of the spring gets the first choice, and that you are not the first boat.
The errand done

Dorestad, the count's hall. The steward has the tally of what your house owes on a nail by the door, and beside it a shorter stick: the errand. He holds out his hand for whatever came back from the far shore.

A count's timber hall at Dorestad: a steward with a ring of keys standing by a door post where two tally sticks hang on a nail, his hand held out, a Frisian skipper unwrapping a string of honey-coloured beads from a scrap of fleece.
The count's lady has asked three times whether the Frisian is home. I said the far shore is further than Colonia. She called that no answer. What have you?
Matched, clear and drilled. She will wear it to Mass at Easter, and the abbess will count the beads. That is what it is for.
Raw lumps. Well. Somebody here can cut it, and she will have to wait. The count dislikes it when she waits.
Lay the matched string in his hand
Set the sack of raw stone on his table
Say the stone is promised elsewhere, and leave the errand open

He holds the string to the light of the door, and for once says nothing about what you owe. The short stick comes off the nail and is broken across his knee. The long one stays. The toll man will be told to look kindly on your boat for a season.
He weighs the sack in his hand and sends a boy for the comb-maker, who cuts bone and may cut this. The short stick comes off the nail. It is an errand done, he says, if not done handsomely.
He looks at the short stick on the nail, and then at you. It can hang there, he says. Sticks keep. So do counts' ladies, but not as well.
A fast only he can count

The Dane's long house, the hearth lit, pork on a spit and mead going round. At the end of the bench a thin man in a short Frisian cloak has a bowl of smoked bream and nothing else, and is counting something on his fingers.

The inside of a thatched long house by firelight: pork on a spit and men with horn cups along the bench, and at the far end a thin man in a short cloak with a wooden cross on a thong, a bowl of smoked fish before him, counting on his fingers; a broad Dane offering him a rib and grinning.
You speak like the Rhine mouth. Say something else. Anything. I have not heard it since my father stopped talking.
The only other baptised skipper on the lake. Sit by me, so that the Dane has two of us to laugh at.
A fast day, by my count. I asked the fishers when Easter falls. They told me when the ice goes, so I count from that. Am I right?
The Frisian eats fish on days only he can count. I have asked him who is watching. He says that is the point. Pork?
They give a marten skin for a wool cloak here, and think they have robbed you. Bring cloth. Bring all the cloth there is.
My half of the stick is in my belt. Four bolts, before this day next year. The marten will be sorted: dark ones. I know what the Rhine pays.
A Svea who lodges here keeps an English boy who tallies for him. The boy crossed himself when he saw my cross, and then looked at his master.
Keep the fast with him, and tell him the day by your own count
Cut a tally with him: your cloth east, his marten west
Eat the Dane's pork, and say the sea excuses a sailor

Smoked bream and water. You tell him the day as the priests at home would have it, and he is two days out: he lost a Sunday somewhere in the winter. He counts forward again from yours, twice, and is content.
He splits a hazel stick down its length and cuts the same notches across both halves: four bolts east, a timber of marten west. Your half, his half. Then one of you at least must come back, he says.
The pork is good, and the Dane is pleased. Wigmar says nothing and finishes his fish. Afterwards he says the Our Father under his breath, for both of you, and lets you hear him do it.
Eleven and five

The Dane's long house by rushlight, after the others have gone to their benches. A Gotland skipper kneels at the foot of a house post with a small leather purse, and Ketil has asked for a witness from outside the shore. He is pointing at you.

By rushlight, a man kneeling at the foot of a house post, lowering a small leather purse into a hole; on the floor beside him ten thin silver coins and one thick one with a crowned head; an old Dane holding the light and looking away, a Frisian counting on his fingers.
Eleven whole and five cut. Count them with me. One is thick and old, with a king's head. A Svea gave it me for luck. Nothing yet.
A guest's post is a guest's post. This house does not dig under one. But a house can fall, and a witness is how a thing is remembered then.
I go up the Vistula with a boatload of blades. If I am not back by the second ice, tell a woman on Gotland's north shore. Nobody else.
Count them with him, and stand witness
Say you would rather not know where another man's silver sleeps

You count them with him: eleven, and five pieces. The purse goes into the hole and the earth is trodden flat. Ketil cuts nothing on a stick. He says your house's name once, to the post, so that the house knows it.
Ketil shrugs and wakes a comb-maker instead. The Gotlander looks at you a moment longer than is polite. He goes up the river in the morning, and you do not see him again.
A guest's post

The long house, older now, its thatch nearly to the ground. A woman with a bow-drill in her lap and an old round scale case at her belt looks up from a bead, and then at the mark cut on your sea chest.

Inside an old thatched long house: a fair-haired woman of middle years with oval brooches and a bow-drill in her lap pointing with the drill at the foot of one house post, an old round bronze scale case at her belt, a Frisian skipper standing with his cap in his hand.
A Frisian house. Wait. My grandfather had a Frisian who stood witness at a post, in his last summers. Was that yours?
I know which post. We do not dig under a guest's post. But your house was the witness, and a witness may say whose it is now.
He went up the Vistula and did not come down. Nobody has asked for it. On Gotland somebody may still be waiting to be told.
Say it is his, and that a son may yet come for it
Dig it with her as witness, and carry it to Gotland
Dig it, and keep it

It stays under the post. She nods as if you had passed something. Lodging and a place for your chest are yours in this house for good, she says, and her children will be told the mark. The purse will outlast the house.

She holds the light and you dig. Eleven whole and five cut, as the house remembered. She weighs it and says the weight aloud, so that two houses know it. Now it is yours to carry, she says, and not yours to keep.
About forty pennies' weight of silver, one piece of it thick and old. Asfrid says nothing. The next time you ask for your sea chest out of her store, she has trouble finding it.
The wood nobody cuts

South of the houses the alders stand in black water, old and uncut, though the town fetches its firewood from much farther off. A path of laid branches goes in a little way and stops at a spring, and a small upright woman in a grey shawl is standing on it.

Old alders standing in black water, a path of laid branches ending at a spring hung with rags of cloth: a small upright old woman in a grey shawl pinned with a bronze spiral barring the path, a sailor with an armful of green wood stopped in front of her, the skipper behind him.
Somebody cut a branch. Not one of ours. One of yours. Stand there. Do not put it down, and do not put it on a fire.
The one whose man cut wood here. It was put right. The alders have said nothing since. Stand there anyway.
The geese went early. Cut your ice thick this winter, or do not die in summer.
From the woman who is asked, on the Cori's shore. We never met. She sends the root for the belly. I send the one for sleep. Give it here.
Lay the wood back at the spring, with four pennies' weight beside it
Have your man carry it back in, and say nothing
Give her the bundle of dried root from the Cori's shore
Stand where she says, and wait to be looked at

Your man carries the wood back in and lays it by the spring, and you lay cut silver beside the bowl. She looks at the silver as at a thing left by a tide. Then she steps off the path. Nothing more is said about it, by anyone.
Your man carries it back in with a red face and comes out with wet feet. She counts him as he passes. The crew eat cold fish that night, and he is told why by each of the others in turn.

She unties the bundle, smells it and puts it inside her shawl. A twist of something grey comes out in exchange: for sleep, a pinch in hot water. Your men sleep that night like the dead of some other country.
She looks at you for as long as it takes to count you. Then she looks at the trees. You are not sent away, and you are not asked in.
Told in order

The long house at evening. An Englishman of about forty with a string of rough amber on his wrist sits at the hearth counting lands on his fingers, and a Danish woman with oval brooches is drilling a bead and listening to everything.

The long house at evening: an Englishman of forty with a string of rough amber on his wrist counting on his fingers; across the hearth a Frisian skipper talking; a Danish woman with oval brooches drilling a bead and listening to both.
Seven days and nights from the Heaths, under sail all the way. The Wends' land to starboard the whole time. You came the same road?
Your house has been coming here longer than anyone I have met. Sit down. I have questions, and I will pay for the mead.
To port Langeland, Lolland, Falster and Skane, and those are the Danes'. Then Bornholm, with a king of its own. Then Blekinge, More, Oland and Gotland: the Svear's.
The Estmere is broad: the best part of a day to cross under oars. I had a man in the bow with a pole the whole way.
The king and the richest men drink mares' milk; the poor and the slaves drink mead. No ale is brewed. I asked twice.
At one fort they brew ale, and say a Frisian taught them, three lifetimes back. Everywhere else, mares' milk and mead. I shall say it was one fort.
They say the dead lie here a month, a king half a year, and do not rot. I should like to see how before I say so.
The swiftest horse takes the largest heap. That is why a fast horse here costs more than seems reasonable anywhere else.
He remembers things in rows, like beads on a string. Tell him a thing out of its place and he puts it back.
Say what you saw, and say separately what you were told.
If you are ever in the west and a king asks you about this shore, tell it in order. Kings lose patience otherwise.
Tell him what your house saw and no more, and take him up to the palings
Improve on it: bigger heaps, colder cold, a king dead a full year
Say a house's knowledge is its stock, and sell him a sack of amber (45 d)
Let him list the lands to port, and correct nothing

You tell him what your house saw and no more: the month in the house, the heaps along the road, the riding. Next day you stand with him at the palings while a rich man burns. He says each thing over once, in order, and does not write, because he cannot.
He listens, thanks you, and keeps only what the woman tells him afterwards. Half a year, he says in the end; and: sometimes. She gives you a look as dry as her drill.
He buys the sack at a fair price for the English market and rubs one piece on his sleeve, as he has seen done. He asks you nothing more. He will learn it anyway, more slowly.
He lists the lands to port like knots on a rope, and then the lands to starboard. He has every one right. It is the passage you came by, and you could not have said it half so straight.
In on a rope

Where the river leaves the lake: a gap in the reeds marked by nothing at all, fish traps of withy on either side. A weathered man in a sealskin cap stands in a log boat with a sounding pole twice his height, and holds up a hand for you to stop.

A narrow lane of brown water between walls of reed, a ship being hauled through it on a rope by men on the bank, a fisherman in her bow with a tall sounding pole; behind, thatched roofs and a new earth bank.
Stop there. You draw too much. Give me the pole and your steersman's ear, and do what I say when I say it.
The house with the old mark on its sail. Your grandfather came up to the houses under oars. You will go in on a rope.
A hand less water than at the last thaw. The river that feeds the Estmere is dropping its mud at our door.
They have built a harbour at the Vistula's mouth, with a wall. The Gutes go there now. It is nearer the sea by a day.
A shaved man with a book came among the forts after the thaw. They killed him. A duke paid his weight in gold for what was left.
Your stakes are standing. Two came out in the ice, and I set them again. Ships that would have turned back came up to the houses this year.
It burned in one night. Arrows first, then fire. I was on the water. Do not ask me who. I counted boats, not faces.
Pay the fishers to stake and clear the channel (30 d)
Give him the pole, and go in on his word (3 d)
Ask what he knows of the shaved man with the book
Lie in the river mouth, and send the small boat in

Alder stakes with withy tops, driven down both sides of the way through the reeds, and the weed cut between them. The fishers do it in four days. For two springs a sea-going ship can come up to the houses again, and it is known whose silver did it.
He stands in your bow and says left, and left, and now, in rough Norse, and you are through the reeds with a hand's breadth under you. He counts the boats on the shore under his breath the whole way.

He tells it as he tells the depth of water: a man with a shaved head and a book, after the thaw; killed, somewhere among the forts; bought back by a duke, weight for weight in gold. He thinks the duke will want more than a body for that gold.
You lie in the river mouth among the fish traps and send the small boat in. It is slower by a day. The fishers look at every bale that goes past them, and say nothing.
Raking the ash

A strip of blackened turf between the houses and the river, with low mounds along the bank. Women go over a cold pyre with wooden rakes, slowly, looking for bone, and a pot stands ready. The Dane from the long house has come down to your boat, which he does not usually do.

A strip of blackened turf by a slow river with low green mounds along the bank: three women going over a cold pyre with wooden rakes, a clay pot standing ready, a Dane in a blue cloak beckoning a southern skipper up from his boat.
They want a stranger's eyes. A man with no kin on this shore cannot have looked away. Walk the ash with them and say what you see.
You walked the ash for them once and said what you saw. They have not forgotten. Nor has the fort. It likes a man who can be asked.
Here every man is burnt, of whatever people. If one bone is found whole afterwards, his kin pay for it, and they pay heavily. So they rake.
My man's brother. He drowned off the west shore with his net. The sea had him three days. Wet men burn badly. That is why we look twice.
Your baptised men will not come past the last house. The others have taken their caps off without being told.
Walk the ash behind the rakes, and say what you see
Lay four pennies' weight in the pot for the kin (4 d)
Stand off at the edge of the turf, with your cap in your hand

You walk the black turf from end to end behind the rakes. Ash, charcoal, a knife gone blue, a few rivets. No bone bigger than a bean. You say so aloud in your own tongue, and the Dane says it in theirs. The eldest woman puts a lump of sea-stone in your hand without looking at you.

Near the middle a rake turns up a thigh bone, black outside and whole. Everyone stops. You say what you see, since that is what you were asked for. The kin will pay for it, the Dane says quietly, and heavily. They asked for a stranger's eyes, and they had them.
Four pennies' weight goes into the pot that waits for the bones. Nobody thanks you. One of the women moves the pot a hand's breadth nearer the pyre, which the Dane says is thanks.
You stand at the edge of the black turf with your cap off. The rakes go on. The wind brings the smell of wet ash and, from the old green mounds along the bank, nothing.
Antler and green glass

A plot heaped with antler: tines in one pile, sawn plates in another, white dust underfoot. A man rivets tooth-plates between two bars. Next door a woman winds a thread of green glass round an iron rod over a clay hearth, and a bead grows on it.

A craftsman's plot heaped with antler, white dust underfoot: a man riveting a comb between two bars at a bench, and beside him a woman winding green glass round an iron rod over a small clay hearth, strings of beads on a peg.
Count the teeth. Thirty to a comb, cut after the plates are riveted, not before. A man who cuts first is selling you firewood with a handle.
I am short of antler. The Este bring it when they have nothing else to do, which is never in summer. Red deer, shed, not sawn off.
The Svear take my combs east by the hundred and sell them for a skin apiece, I am told. I should like to see that skin.
Have you broken glass? Any colour. I pay in beads or in silver, and I pay more than they do on Gotland. Do not tell them I said so.
Buy a bundle of combs at the bench (8 d)
Sell him a load of antler (9 d)
Sell her a sack of raw glass (28 d)
Watch a comb riveted, and buy nothing

A bundle of combs in their cases, tied with bast, the teeth even and the rivets flush. He counts them into your hands and makes you count them back. On the eastern river, he has heard, one of them buys a squirrel skin.
He turns each beam over, raps it, and sets the best aside for long combs. Nine pennies' weight, paid at once in cut silver that the Dane weighed for him this morning.

She tips the sack out on a hide and sorts it by colour before she pays: green here, blue there, the clear in a pot by itself. Twenty-eight pennies' weight. More than Gotland gives, she says, and she is right.

He drills, sets the rivet and strikes it once. The saw goes through three plates at a stroke, and the teeth come out even. White dust settles on your sleeves. Nobody minds your watching: it is slow work, and company shortens it.
This year after Easter a bishop of the Bohemians went among the Bruzi to preach, and they killed him. A duke of the Poles bought the body for its weight in gold.
Follow the pole

A long low coast of pale sand with surf standing on it and no haven anywhere. In one place the surf is broken, and brown water runs out through it over a bar. A flat-bottomed boat lies there with a wiry man standing in it, holding a sounding pole twice his height.

A long low coast of pale sand with surf standing on it and dark pines behind: a gap of brown water running out over a bar, a flat-bottomed boat with a wiry sunburnt man standing in it holding a sounding pole twice his height, a small trading boat hove to outside the broken water.
Small boat. Good. Deep? No. Good. You follow my pole, not your eyes. Your eyes are for another sea.
The small boat. I saw your sail and knew the mast. The water has moved since you were here. Follow me again.
A Gotlander came in on his own last spring, by the old way. We dug him out with spades. He paid double, and said nothing.
You sleep at the widow's house. Then no silver. Do not tell her I said so. She likes me to be asked.
Three ships out this moon, all low. Furs do not sit a ship so low. I do not ask.
The lake skins over in one night. I have walked home across water I poled that morning. Go soon.
Stone? In that boat? Over my bar? Wait here. I go to fetch men with ropes. And I shall laugh the whole way there and back.
Give him a sack of salt, and follow his pole
Give him three pennies' weight of silver, and follow his pole
Follow his pole as the widow's guest, and ask him nicely
Thank him, and feel your own way in by the old channel
He hefts the sack, grins and goes ahead in his flat boat. When his pole goes up, you row; when he shouts, you row harder. You touch nothing. Salt keeps, he says. Silver only gets counted.
He takes the silver without looking at it and goes ahead. When his pole goes up, you row. You are over the bar and into the lake with a hand's breadth under you.
He will take nothing from a man who sleeps on the widow's bench, and is pleased to have been asked all the same. He goes ahead, and you follow the pole.

You feel your way in on last year's marks and a great deal of luck, with your steersman calling the colour of the water. The pilot watches from his boat and says nothing. Tonight he will tell it as a story about fools, and how some of them float.

The channel is not where it was. You stick fast in the surf with the lake in sight, and men come out with spades. It costs double, and a bruised crew. The pilot does not say that he told you. He only tells you again.
Weighed twice

Open-fronted booths on ground so dark with old hearths that it stains the shoes. A plank on two trestles, a folding balance, a heap of rough amber. A lean Gotlander stands on one side of the plank and a tall Curonian with a notched staff on the other, and each looks at you as if the other were not there.

A plank on trestles on black ground under a fort hill: a lean Gotlander and a tall Curonian with a neck ring on either side of a folding balance, rough amber in one pan and cut silver in the other, and a Frisian merchant between them holding the beam level with one finger.
A Frisian. I have heard of you and not seen one. Put your silver on the pan, and we will find out how far you came.
You are back, and the bar let you in again. Good. I kept the large pieces by. Weigh first, then tell me the news.
You are welcome here, stranger. It may be we have what you want, and you what we want. Silver is a fine thing. You cannot plough with it.
The Frisian with the small boat. My son said you would come back. He has been practising your numbers. He is not yet good.
I weigh your pennies and give you a number. He weighs them on his own beam and gives you a smaller. Then we both look at you.
The stranger has a scale of his own, with weights neither of us poured. It may be that such a scale has no cousins on this bank.
When the Frisian is in, the amber goes on the Frisian's beam. When he is not, we split the difference and call it the Frisian's share. Nobody collects it.
The Svea on the hill says the Curonians owe tribute. His grandfather took it. He has eleven men. I have counted them more often than he has.
A Dane you know weighs at the next plank, for another man. He kept his own house at the Este's lake until a guest robbed a burning.
Weigh on the Gotlander's scale, and buy a sack of amber at his number (20 d)
Take the Curonian's weighing, and pay in iron tools for two sacks
Set your own scale on the plank, and stand by its reading
Watch them weigh for others, and learn both numbers

He weighs slowly and gives you his number, and it is fair. Among his cut silver lies half a coin, white, with writing all round and no king's head. He will not sell it. He lets you hold it. The Curonian carries his next basket past the plank without stopping.
The Curonian weighs on a beam with a stone for a weight, and gives you two sacks for the crate of tools. It may be remembered, he says. The Gotlander says only that he hopes you got good weight.

You set your own balance on the plank. The Gotlander tries it against his. The Curonian tries it against a stone from his belt. Neither says anything for some time. Then the amber is weighed on it, and both of them watch your finger and not each other.
You stand a morning at the plank and learn both numbers for everything on it. They differ by about a tenth. Neither man thinks the other a cheat. Each thinks the other's scale was poured by one.
A bench turned to the wall

The longest house on the black earth: a hearth down the middle, sleeping benches with sheepskins along both walls, a loom by the door where the light is. A small straight woman in island brooches counts your crew as they duck under the lintel, and counts cups to match.

The inside of a long timber house: a hearth down the middle, sheepskin-covered benches along both walls, a loom by the door, a small straight woman with animal-head brooches and a string of beads pouring ale and counting cups, a wet crew coming in under the lintel.
Four men and a small boat. You came over the bar in that? Then you have earned the bench by the fire. Ale first. Names when you are dry.
Your bench is kept. The steersman's too, by the wall, where he likes it. One of you owes me for a cup. I forget which.
You look at my roof as if it should not be there. What have they been telling you at Birka?
A stone with two birds stands in the men's field. I want its twin for my grave. I have the silver, weighed twice, and nobody who cuts stone.
You have my bag, and my birds on a strip of bark. The stone-cutter is on the island's west shore. So are my mother's kin, whom I never saw.
It stands by my door, and goes with me when the time comes. Your bench is turned to the wall when you leave, so that nobody else warms it.
My mother wore these brooches, and her mother before. Nobody here can cast the like. When they break I shall have to become a Curonian.
Your old Northman set me a riddle before you were a merchant. Tell him I am still thinking, and that it is ill-mannered to live so long.
Take her bag of silver and a drawing of the two birds, for a stone cut on Gotland
Carry the stone up from the boat to her door
Tell her what the Dane at Birka said about this place
Take the bench by the fire, and pay for the cups

She walks you to the old stone among the mounds. A strip of birch bark, a burnt stick, and whichever of your men has the steadiest hand: two birds, facing, the size they are. Then her bag of silver, weighed twice before your eyes. Sixty pennies' weight.

Four men and a rope get it over the bar and up the bank. She puts her hand flat on the two birds and says nothing for a while. Then she sets it by her door, gives you the bench by the fire for good, and two sacks of amber she had been keeping for something.
Burnt? She laughs until she has to sit. Somebody at Birka wanted the amber for himself, she says. It is the oldest trick on this sea, and she will wager it had a Dane's beard. It did.

Ale, smoked fish, and a sheepskin by the fire. She asks after each of your men by the bench he slept on last time. In the morning the pilot is eating her eels at the end bench, and has been told you are not to be charged.
The old tribute

A steep path up the spit to a gap in a fence of upright logs. Two men sit in the gap with spears across their knees and a board game between them. A broad man with a square red-brown beard gets up, and walks you a little way along the bank where the others cannot hear.

The gap in a log fence on a steep spit at evening: a broad Svea with a square beard and a tall Curonian with a notched staff facing each other across a bundle in sailcloth lying on the ground, the merchant standing behind it, the river and the booths small below.
A trader from the Franks' river. You will have iron, then. I do not ask what kind. A sword fetches three times its price here, in pelts.
You again. Good. The hill is still ours, as you see. Count the men at the gate if you like. I do, every morning.
A Frisian promised me blades through a Dane, two summers ago. I have the Dane's word and the Frisian's name. Neither cuts.
My father's father took a pelt from every hearth between here and the amber shore. I take what the Gotlander's guests leave in the cup.
I walked down to speak of the weather. What did the man on the hill ask of you? My people would pay in amber, and pay more.
You sit low, and it is not furs. Each of us has a man watching the other's door. Tonight you tell one of us yes.
Sell three swords to the Svea on the hill, for pelts
Sell three swords to the Curonians, for amber
Tell both men to their faces that you sell no swords here
Say you will think on it, and go down to the booths

Three swords go up the path under a cloak, and twenty timbers of grey squirrel come down it by night. The Svea asks for the tribute at the next thaw. For a year or two he gets some of it. The Curonians do not forget who armed the hill.

Three swords go inland in a basket of eels, and twenty sacks of amber come down to the bank before dawn. Nothing happens that summer. In the autumn the Svea counts the spears at the bank, counts his own, and takes a Gotland ship home with his men and his name.

Both are angry for a season. The hill will change hands anyway, slowly and with shouting, because eleven men cannot keep it. No king's man on the Rhine will ever have cause to ask what you carried east.
The Svea nods and goes back to his game. On the way down, the Curonian happens to be walking the same path, and speaks of the weather.
The woman who is asked

A small round-cornered house at the edge of the hornbeams, apart from the rest, with bunches of dry plants under the eaves and a fire that is never let out. An old woman sits on the threshold with her hands in her lap. People wait at the fence to be looked at.

A small round-cornered house under old hornbeams with bunches of dry plants hanging from the eaves: a bent old woman with two white plaits and a string of rough amber sitting on the threshold with her hands in her lap, people waiting at a fence, a foreign skipper standing in the light before her.
Sit. No, there, in the light. You came to ask a thing. First you ask the wrong thing. They all do. I will wait.
The one from the west river. Your man with the cough, he lives? Good. Then you owe me nothing, and you have come to ask again.
You would ask who wins, the hill or the forts. I answer otherwise. A sword sold to either will be used. Sold to neither, a worse man sells it.
You told both of them no. The worse man I spoke of has not come. It surprises me. Ask what you like today. I take nothing for it.
Your people have one god, I hear, and he is jealous. Ours are many, and they are busy. I do not know which is worse for a trader.
At the Este's lake a woman is asked. She sends me the root for sleep; I send the one for the belly. The amber boats carry it. Yours could.
Ask her for something for a sick man aboard, for a string of beads
Take her bundle of dried root for the woman at the lake of the Este
Ask her whether the water will let you out today

She looks at the man before she looks at the beads. A handful of dried leaves, to be boiled and drunk hot, and a few words in her own tongue to go with it that she does not translate. He is on his feet in three days.
A bundle of grey roots tied with bast, light as a bird. She tells you whom it is for and nothing else. If it comes to the other woman dry, something will come back the same way.
Go, she says. The water will take you out or it will not. That one she does not answer. Ask the man with the pole.
A gift at the gate

The hill is the Curonians' now, and a spear stands in the gap of the log fence where the board game used to be. A tall man in a blue tunic with a folding balance at his belt meets every stranger at the foot of the path, and does not smile until something has been laid down.

The foot of a steep path below a log-fenced hill, a spear standing in the gap above: a tall man in a blue tunic with a bronze neck ring and a folding balance at his belt holding out an open hand, a Frisian skipper setting down a bundle of iron bars at his feet.
A gift at the gate, then the plank. That is the custom now. Your father's house may have known another. This is the one that holds.
I know your boat. My father knew your house. Lay the gift down and never mind the speech. What do you carry?
I count a guest's days aloud, so that he hears the last one coming. You have seven. This is the first.
My father said it might be remembered, and it is. For your house the gate asks nothing, and nobody counts your days. Do not tell the Gotlanders.
Your house armed the hill, in my father's time. We have long memories and a short list. It is nothing against you. It is against your grandfather.
My father never said no to a stranger. I say it twice a day. The amber is the same price.
The gales have thrown the stone up thick this autumn. My people bring it down in baskets. It is cheap until the lake skins over. Then no boat.
A Birka man asks me how many we are inside the fence. I ask him how many oars his king has. Neither of us answers.
Lay a bundle of bar iron at the gate
Lay eight pennies' weight of silver at the gate
Walk up as your house has leave to
Lay nothing down, and trade from the boat with whoever comes

He lifts the bundle, counts the bars and laughs once, loudly, which with him means it is true weight. Seven days at the plank, counted aloud. Iron, he says, is the one gift nobody here has ever sent back.
He weighs it on his own balance where you can see, and it is enough. Seven days at the plank. He would rather have had iron, and says so.
You walk up without laying anything down, and the man with the spear stands aside. Wissegerde says nothing about it. He simply does not count.
Nobody stops you. A few come down to the bank with baskets and sell you what the plank did not want. Up at the gate your days are not counted, because you were never a guest.
Danish gold, sold like fish

The market is full of Danish things: ring silver, shields, a gilt cup with a cross on its foot, and long ships for sale on the lake shore with nobody to row them. The grey Curonian who keeps the plank is selling the gold fast, as if it were fish.

A market on black earth under a fort hill crowded with spoil: shields stacked like plates, ring silver on a hide, a gilt cup with a cross on its foot standing on a plank, a grey Curonian in a blue tunic holding a folding balance, long ships drawn up empty on a lake shore behind.
The Danes came with many ships and went home with half. The five towns met them together. The other half lies on our shore. Will you buy a ship?
There is gold in the market this year, crosses on some. The Danes took it from someone. Someone will come to take it from us. So I sell.
All my life I have been told the Svear will come back. I count sails from the dunes. This year I cannot sleep for counting.
You know something this man has feared all his life. He does not know that you know it.
Buy the gilt cup with the cross on its foot (90 d)
Tell him at the gate what the young men at Birka are saying
Say nothing at the gate, and take whoever will come from the bank over the bar
Trade, and say nothing to anyone

A gilt cup with a cross on its foot, weighed as so much silver and sold as so much less. It has been stolen twice and bought once. Some church on your own river will know what it is, and what it is worth to have it back.

He listens without moving. Then he asks why a guest of the Svear would tell him so, and looks at you for a long time, and believes you. He does not thank you. Before the next moon the people of the bank are inland, behind the second fort's fence.

Eleven people and a loom, in a boat built for four men. The pilot walks ahead of you in the water to his chest. You are to set them down on Gotland, where a widow's farm will take them in. Behind you the town still stands, and its fighting men are in it.
You buy and sell and say nothing. The gold goes fast. On the lake shore the Danish ships lie in a row with weed already on them, and children play at rowing.
Smoke over the pines

From the sea, smoke stands over the pines behind the dunes, a great deal of it. No boat lies at the outlet. A sounding pole is stuck upright in the sand where the brown water runs out, and beside it sits a boy of twelve, who gets up when he sees your mast.

A pale sand shore seen from the sea: thick smoke standing over dark pines behind the dunes, brown water running out over a bar, a tall sounding pole stuck upright in the sand, and beside it a boy of twelve standing up, one hand raised.
My father's pole. He said: stand it where the water runs, so that the next boat knows. Then he went back for my mother. The town is gone.
The men from the ships went five days inland, to the fort at the river, and took silver for every head. From here they took nothing. Nothing was left.
The bank's people went inland before the ships. The old one at the plank said a guest told him. He left this for your mast. No speech, he said.
You took eleven over the bar the night before. My aunt was one. She says your name is not a name in our tongue, so she remembers the mast.
Take what was left at the pole for a boat with your mast
Take the boy aboard: he knows every bar on this coast
Leave him bread and a knife, and stand out to sea
Six sacks of amber under a hide weighted with stones, sorted, the large pieces on top. No mark and no message. He said no speech, the boy says again, in case you had been about to make one.

He pulls the pole out of the sand and brings it aboard with him. It is twice his height. He looks at the smoke once and then at the water, and before you are clear of the bar he has told your steersman twice that he is wrong.
A loaf, a knife and a fire-steel. He takes them without a word and sits down again by the pole. Somebody has to stand it where the water runs, he says, so that the next boat knows.
The women's ground

A level stretch of sandy turf by a stand of old hornbeams, with nothing on it but small ringed patches where the grass grows greener. No mounds, no stones. The widow from the long house kneels at one of the patches with a cup in her hand.

A level stretch of sandy turf by old hornbeams, small ringed patches of greener grass and no mounds or stones: a small upright widow with island brooches on her dress kneeling to pour from a cup, a southern skipper at the edge of the trees with his cap in his hand.
My husband's sister. I pour her milk, since she never cared for ale. Do not stand on the green patches. They are the only doors these houses have.
We are laid here in our brooches, the island's kind, so that we are known. The men go to the mounds with their swords. Nobody mistakes which is which.
There are fewer of us each year to pour. The young ones marry into the forts and are laid their way. I do not blame them. I count them.
You carry beads. She liked blue. A string laid here goes with her, and I should think better of a Frisian than I have had cause to.
Lay a string of glass beads at the green patch
Take the cup when she holds it out, and pour
Stand at the edge of the trees, with your cap off

A string of blue goes down on the green patch, and she presses it into the sand with the flat of her hand until it is gone. Glass keeps, she says. Bone does not, and names do not. She tells you the dead woman's name anyway.

Milk, a little sour. You pour it where she points, and the sand takes it at once. She nods. A stranger's hand is as good as another, she says. The dead are not particular about who, only about whether.

A lark, the smoke of the settlement beyond the hornbeams, and a small woman kneeling at a patch of greener grass. She does not look round. When she passes you on the path she says: you stood still. Most cannot.
Now you pay, now I show

A narrow side river running into a broad brown one under a low bank of clay. Sea ships lie nose to the mud with their masts down. A short, very wide-shouldered man with a sounding pole taller than himself has come up from the fort at the stream mouth to look at how deep you sit.

A low clay bank where a narrow side river meets a broad brown one: sea ships nosed to the mud with their masts down, river boats and dugouts in a row, a short very wide-shouldered man in a long linen shirt and bast shoes with a sounding pole taller than himself, looking at a small Frisian boat's waterline.
You draw too much water. Not for the river: for the lake shore. Next time, come in behind me. Now you pay, now I show.
Frisian. The boat is whole. Good. You listened, or the lake was asleep. Which? No matter. Same price.
The ice sang last night. Thin song. Twelve days and it goes, or I give you back the iron.
Up where the river is born, it runs backwards some years. Into its own lake. Three days, four. I saw it. You do not believe. Good. Cheaper for me.
The stream at our wall fills with mud. My father tied his boat at the gate. I tie mine forty steps out. My son will walk.
The Svear tell me their own pilot at home reads water better. I ask: has his water rocks in it? They go quiet.
My sister's son went into the pen behind the big house, and south. I take the big man's ships up at full price, and look at the water.
Give him a bundle of bar iron to show you the lake shore and the river
Give him a sack of salt to show you the lake shore and the river
Ask him for the marks of the south shore, for good
Hear him out about the river that runs backwards

He takes the iron, tries its weight in one hand, and walks you down the bank pointing. Here shoal. There shoal. That colour of water, go back. Then up the river as far as the noise of the rocks, and where the bales are carried.
He tastes the salt, nods, and walks you down the bank pointing. Here shoal. There shoal. When the water goes white ahead, turn left. He says it three times in two tongues.

A dead pine, a white stone and the smoke of his own fort, in that order, with the lake's south shore on your right hand. He scratches it in the clay with his pole and then treads it out. Now you have it, he says, and your sons.
He tells it again: the river running back into its own lake, for days. Your crew laugh. He laughs too, suddenly, and stops. He is right, as it happens, and has given up minding.
A bead for a pelt

A strip of trodden ground between the houses and the water. Skins lie in tied bundles of forty, stacked like firewood. Men in fur caps from the woods stand a little apart, and a small straight-backed woman with bronze spirals on her apron stands between them and you.

A trodden river bank under a low white sky: a blanket on the ground with a string of blue eye beads on it, a small dark-haired woman with bronze spirals on her apron holding up four fingers to three men in fur caps, a foreign merchant beside her, bundles of skins stacked behind.
They ask who you are and what you carry. I told them: a stranger, with cloth. They ask to feel the cloth. That is a good sign.
The men remember your cloth. It lasted the winter. They brought the better skins down for you, and I did not tell them to.
They call you the glass man. When they hear your boat is in, the winter fur comes down. I lay my blanket where your boat lies.
Your pennies they hand back. Nobody here knows the king on them. The woods want beads, iron and cloth, in that order. The beads are made forty steps away.
Forty skins is forty in every tongue. It is only the price that needs translating. I count aloud in three, so that nobody can say he misheard.
Squirrel will be thick this winter. The cones were heavy. Buy your beads now, green ones, before the big house hears it.
A trapper asked why the white silver has scratches and no face. I said the men who make it have a god who dislikes faces. He approved.
On other rivers the Northmen take a skin from each hearth and call it peace. Here they still pay. I count every summer that they do.
Lay a string of beads on the blanket, for a timber of squirrel
Lay three strings of beads on the blanket, for a timber of marten
Lay a bolt of woollen cloth on the blanket, for beaver
Stand where she puts you, and let them look

She counts aloud in three tongues. A string of beads goes one way across the blanket and a timber of grey squirrel comes the other, forty skins tied by the heads. The trapper holds one bead up to the sky and looks through the eye.

With three strings on the blanket the trappers come close. The skins they bring out now are not the ones they showed you before: dark marten, forty to the bundle. You are the first stranger, she says, to pay the woods' own price without being told it twice.
They feel the cloth, pull at the weave and nod. A bundle of ten beaver skins comes across the blanket. Wine they laugh at, she says. They tried it once. Cloth they understand.
They look at your boots, your knife and your crew, in that order, and say something that makes her smile. She does not translate it. She says: come with beads.
The man with the scale

One long house among the cabins, built the old Northern way. A broad man in a fur-lined cap sits near the door where the light is, a folding scale in front of him and a leather bag of thin white coins at his knee. Behind the house there is a pen of split logs, and somebody coughing in it.

Inside a long timber house by the open door: a broad heavy man in a fur-lined cap with a folding scale before him and a leather bag of thin white coins at his knee, three rings on a hand missing its smallest finger, bundles of skins hanging from the rafters, a foreign merchant on the bench opposite.
A new boat. Sit, friend. Nobody takes a toll here. I only like to know what comes up my river. Now, what is under that sailcloth?
The Frisian. I told them it was your boat when she was still a speck. Sit where you sat before. The scale has missed you.
Bring me blades. Bare, no hilts, the kind with the pattern in the iron. For those I pay the white silver, and I do not make you wait.
The silver was thin this year. They say the king on the great river took more than his tenth. Skins are cheap, so buy now and say nothing.
Does Holmfast know you are here? I ask as a friend. He will ask me the same of you, as a friend, and I shall tell him.
I once offered Holmfast a timber of sable for his English tally-boy. Not for sale by weight, he said. I thought the price fair. I think so still.
A Gotlander came across the lake alone, no Svea with him, in a night calm. A fine seaman, or a lucky one. I should like to know which.
A bronze man who sits with his legs folded? The silver comes from people who allow no images. So he is not theirs. Beyond them I have never been.
Sell him a bolt of Frisian cloth, and be paid in the writing silver (70 d)
Sell him a pair of bare blades (440 d)
Buy a timber of marten at his weighing (84 d)
Sit, and tell him the news of the west

He names a weight, not a price, and pays it at once in thin white coins with writing all round and no face: the first you have been paid in. He watches you look at them. They spend like any silver west of here, he says, if the man has a scale.

He bends each over his knee and lets it spring. Then white silver, weighed out without a pause: nearly four times what the pair cost you on the Rhine. He asks, friend to friend, whether Holmfast knows you are here.

Forty dark skins, tied by the heads, counted by a thin boy with a tally stick who does not look up. He weighs your silver and says the scale has no friends on the day it weighs, and has them all the day after.
You tell him who is king where, and what cloth fetches on the Rhine. He listens with his eyes half shut and forgets none of it. News, he says, is the one cargo that pays no carriage.
Beads that look back

A low cabin with its door propped open for the heat. Inside, a clay hearth no bigger than a cooking fire, and a thin woman with half-singed eyebrows turning a blob of dark glass on an iron rod. Finished beads hang drying on a line of bast, each with a ring of white and a dot, so that it looks back at you.

A low cabin with its door propped open: a thin woman with half-singed eyebrows and her hair under a linen cloth turning a blob of dark glass on an iron rod over a small clay hearth, a line of blue and green eye beads drying on a cord like berries, a merchant holding a sack.
Stand out of my light. Are you buying or looking? Looking, I think. Have you glass? Broken will do. Then you are buying.
The Frisian with the glass. Was I right about the green? I was. The woods took every one. Bring more of it.
One of my eye beads bought a marten skin last winter. One. The man who told me was angry, because he had paid two.
If you see a Birka bead, look at the eye. Crooked. Too much lead. Tell the woman who makes them I said so. She will know who.
The big man wants the trappers at his door and not at Ihalempi's blanket. They will not go. They have seen what is behind his house.
Glass is sand that remembers the fire. So do I, and so does my thatch.
Give her a sack of raw glass for four strings of eye beads
Take her order for glass from the Rhine
Stand out of her light, and watch an eye go in

She tips the sack out, sorts it by colour and is at the rod before you have sat down. Four strings of forty by the time the wind has turned: blue for marten, green for squirrel, the black with yellow eyes for nearly anything.
Three sacks of raw glass, cakes or broken cups, by next summer. She will pay half again what it costs on your river. She asks whether she was right to trust you, and answers that she was.
A thread of white goes round a blob of blue, then a dot of black, and the bead looks back at you. She does it on a fire you could cover with your cap. Nobody north of here knows how.
A corpse on a corpse

The oldest roof in the place, black with sixty winters of soot. Tongs and hammers of a dozen sizes hang in order on pegs. On a shelf above the door sits a bronze man the length of a finger, with two curved horns rising from his head. The smith goes on hammering while he looks at your boat through the door.

Inside a soot-black smithy: a lean smith with a long plaited beard tucked into his belt hammering at a stone-set anvil, tongs and hammers hung in order on pegs, a small horned bronze figure on the shelf above the door, a brown river and a small boat seen through the doorway.
A Frisian boat. Then you have rivets working loose and do not know it yet. Sit. I will tell you which when I have looked.
You again. The rudder iron held, then. I said it would. People are always surprised, and I never know why.
I saw a corpse sit on a corpse, the blind ride the blind toward the sea, and the steed lifeless. Name it, and I say where to dig.
You have it. I saw it in the way you looked at the river. Come to the mounds at dusk. Bring nobody who talks.
The little horned one on the shelf was the top of some older thing. They call it the singer. It rang when the first smith struck it.
My grandfather built this roof. Three houses and a forge, and all Northmen. Then the log-cabin people came. They stayed. We mostly did not.
Bare blades. I can see the bundle. Do you want hilts on them, or do you want to be gone quickly? I do not ask where they came from.
Your grey seaman sat a bench with me one winter on Gotland. He will know my riddle's wording. He will not tell you the answer. He never does.
Have him tighten your loose rivets, and take his riddle away (4 d)
Tell him what went down the river on the ice
Have him fit plain hilts to a pair of bare blades (10 d)
Sit by the forge and watch him work
He tightens four rivets and a rudder iron while your boat waits, and says the riddle over once more with the hammer for a beat. Think about it, he says. The river will remind you.
You tell him: a dead horse on an ice floe, going down to the lake. He nods and goes on hammering to the end of the heat. Then he says: the mounds, at dusk.

A plain guard and a pommel on each, in the fashion of this river, fitted while you wait. He sights down each blade and says nothing about where it was made. After this they are nobody's business but the buyer's.
Iron tells you at the first blow what it will be, he says. Men take longer, and are wrong more often. He does not look up. You are welcome to the bench.
Between two mounds

Dusk, below the town. Steep round hills too regular to be hills stand along the river, grass-grown, and cattle graze their lower slopes and will not go to the top. The smith has walked you to a spot between two of them, and now stands on it.

Dusk on a river bank below a town: steep round grass-grown mounds in a row, cattle on their lower slopes, a lean smith with a plaited beard standing on a spot between two of them and pointing at the ground, a merchant with a spade.
Here. A man with a spade and a quiet evening. Some thirty thin coins, in a bag that will have rotted. I do not watch. I have a forge.
The man who put them there counted them twice, and never came back for them. That is another story, and there is no silver in it.
Dig, and lay a tenth of it at the foot of the nearest mound
Dig, keep it, and tell him only how many
Leave the spade, and ask him for the other story

A rotted bag and some thirty thin white coins. You lay three at the foot of the nearest mound before you go. The smith was watching after all. The ground here is full of people who were promised something, he says. From now on your boat is mended at the cost of the iron.
A rotted bag and some thirty thin white coins. Nobody claims them. The smith asks only how many, nods at the number, and says the man who buried them counted the same.

He is silent for a time, and then tells it: who the man was, where he meant to go, and what he used to say over the fire in the dark months. He cuts you the stanza on a stick. The coins stay where they are.
The one who brings buyers

A little way from the houses, where the bank is highest, a tall post stands in the ground with a face cut in it, and smaller posts round it. Bread, an onion and a strip of dried meat lie at its foot.
