A trader with his cap in his hand is talking to the big post in a low voice, as a man talks to a creditor.

A high river bank at morning: a tall wooden post with a face cut in it and smaller posts round it, bread and an onion at its foot and a dog nosing them, a trader with his cap in his hand speaking low to the big post, a ship's crew stopped at the edge of the grass.
I told him: I come with so many skins, so many people. Send me a buyer with white silver who does not haggle. Then I gave him bread.
Which god? The one who brings buyers. You people from the west always want the name. He has not asked yours.
Your baptised men have stopped at the edge of the grass. The others are feeling in their pouches for something to leave.
Let those of your men who wish leave bread before the lake crossing
Ask the trader what buyers he was sent this year
Walk round the posts, as the path does

Bread, an onion and a strip of dried meat go down at the foot of the post. The baptised men look at the river. Everybody is easier for it in the morning, when the lake is flat and wide and has to be crossed.

He laughs. The post sent him a Svea, which is not what he asked for. Skins are cheap this year, since the silver from the south came thin. He tells you that for nothing, having just been haggled with.
The path bends round the posts, and so do you. A dog has the bread before you are out of sight. Nobody at the post thinks that a bad sign.
Where your boat cannot go

Above the last houses the river narrows between limestone banks, and from the bend comes a steady noise like wind in pines: the first of the rapids. Here the river boats load, men to the thigh in brown water passing bales hand to hand. Nothing with a keel goes further.

A long, low, plank-sided river boat being loaded below limestone banks, men to the thigh in brown water passing bales hand to hand, a short wide-shouldered pilot in the bow with a sounding pole, white water showing at the bend upstream.
A third of this boat is unspoken for. Up past the rocks to the upper lake, down before the frost. I am the pilot, so it comes back.
Cloth and beads and iron go up. Wax and skins come down. Silver, in the good years.
In a year of fighting up there, little comes down, and I come down fast. I say it now, so that you do not say it to me after.
Put a bolt of Frisian cloth and sixty pennies' weight into his boat, for a third
Say your goods go where you can follow them

Your cloth goes amidships under a hide and your silver into his shirt. He splits a stick, cuts both halves alike and gives you one. The boat goes up the bank path on men's shoulders, past the noise of the rocks.
He shrugs. The lake drowns the proud and the river drowns the hurried, he says. A careful man drowns nobody, and buys at the bank price. He does not mean it unkindly.
Down before the frost

The river-boat bank again, and a long shallow hull drawn up on it with her bottom scarred white by rock. The pilot sits on her gunwale with three heaps laid out on a hide, and has plainly been sitting there since he saw your mast.

A long shallow river boat drawn up on a bank with her bottom scarred white by rock: a short wide-shouldered pilot sitting on her gunwale beside three heaps laid out on a hide, yellow wax cakes and bundled dark skins, first frost on the grass.
Down before the frost, as I said. Nothing lost at the rocks. Three heaps. One is yours. Count it in your tongue; I counted it in mine.
Count your third
Two cakes of wax the size of querns, a timber of dark marten and forty pennies' weight of the white silver. More than twice what you put in. He holds out his half of the stick, and the notches meet.

One cake of wax and thirty pennies' weight of silver. There was fighting on the upper river, and he came down fast with what he had. He told you it could be so. The notches on the stick meet all the same.
A stick left for a week's ale

A plank-laid lane along the small river, houses gable-end to the water. Halfway along stands a house twice the length of the others, with a carved door-post and a bench outside worn hollow. Inside, a long fire, sea chests under the benches, and a host who knows what ship each chest came off.

A plank-laid lane along a small river with houses gable-end to the water: the doorway of a house twice the length of the others, a carved door-post and a worn bench, a tall red-bearded host with keys at his belt and a small iron hammer at his neck holding out a rune-cut stick.
A western boat! We do not see many. Put your chest under that bench. Nobody has ever lost one in this house, and I mean to die saying so.
I know that boat's kin. Your father's chest stood under the same bench. Sit. You drink the dark ale, as he did.
A skald left me a stick for his ale. It asks what gives light to every land, and is chased by wolves. Answer, and you drink free.
The Gotlander sent you? Then you are on the road of that door. The Svear king's poet left this for a week's ale. I say I made it.
The next is kept at a river mouth in Skane by a pilot's sister, against an unpaid fare. Then it goes home to the Svear. I keep a house.
The convoy from the south is late. Either the rapids down there were low, or the riders caught them. Silver will be dear until we know.
I was the boy who dug in the ash. Your house bought furs that summer at the old price, with nobody to make it. This bench has your mark.
Your house bought furs here the summer after the fire. I was the boy digging. I remember the price. Sit anywhere. The ale costs what it costs.
Take the skald's stick, and pay for your own ale (2 d)
Tell him what is chased by wolves
Show him a rune stick from your own chest
Put your chest under the bench, and drink the dark ale
He takes it down from the shelf with the tally sticks: a short stick, the runes cut deep by a man in a hurry to drink. You pay for your own ale. The stick goes into your chest.
You say it. He slaps the bench, fills your horn himself, and tells the house he made that riddle. Nobody in the house believes him. Everybody drinks to it.

He reads yours aloud, slowly, tracing each stave with a thumb, and corrects one sound you had wrong. Then he cuts you a stanza in return, one a trader left who wintered here: about a man who had been down to nine worlds, and to the place below them.
Dark ale, fish, wet wool drying by a long fire. He asks your home port, your ship and what you drink, and will know all three in twenty years. Your chest goes under the bench with the others.
Ash on the river

Charred posts, a few lean-tos, the smell of wet ash. Nobody comes down to the boat. A man and a boy are digging where a house stood. On the empty bank three men in fur caps wait beside their bundles, as they do every summer, and there is no scale in the place but yours.

A river bank of black stumps and grey ash under a hard blue sky: a man and a boy of ten digging between charred house posts, a single sea ship with her mast down at the mouth of a side river, and far off on the bank three men in fur caps waiting beside bundles of skins.
My father put the silver under the threshold. We have found the threshold. Who burned it? I was on the river. I know who is left.
The men of the woods have nobody to sell to. Nobody is here to say what a skin is worth but you. They will take what you give.
If you want to do a thing here, bring timber and food before the frost. Not silver. There is nothing to buy with it.
You said timber, before the frost. The boy has counted the days on a burnt stick. I told him a Frisian's days are longer. He did not laugh.
Buy the trappers' marten at last year's price, and help the man dig (80 d)
Buy the furs for what desperate men will take (30 d)
Promise timber and tools from Birka before the frost
Stand off, and go down the river again

You could have had the skins for a third. The trappers know it, and so does the boy. You pay last year's weight and spend two days on a spade. On the fourth day they find a blackened lump of silver, and try to give you half.
The best cargo your house ever carried out of the east, for the least silver. Nobody on the bank says anything. The boy stops digging and watches you load. He will remember the price for a long time.

The man looks at you as at somebody who has said a thing in the wrong tongue. Then he tells the boy. Squared oak, by the frost, at nearly twice what it fetches at home. If it comes, yours will be the first roof on the burned bank.
You go down the river again past the fort at the stream mouth, where a man on the wall shouts to ask whether you have food to sell. Behind you two people go on digging.
A boat on the far bank

Across the great river, on a low terrace opposite the town, they have drawn a boat up on to dry ground and laid a skipper in her with his sea chest, his scales and his dog. His partners stand with torches. Boat rivets from older burnings lie rusting in the grass.

A low river terrace at dusk with small grassed mounds: a clinker boat drawn up on dry ground with a dead man laid in her among his sea chest and gear, a dog at his feet, men standing round with lit torches, the town's roofs and a timber fort small across the wide water.
He came up this river eleven summers and went down it ten. We burn him in his own boat. She was past mending. He would have said so himself.
His scales go with him, folded. His weights we keep. A dead man does not need to be believed. We do.
You are from the west, where they put a man in the ground whole and call it rest. Stand with us, or stand off. Nobody will count it.
Take a torch when it is held out to you
Lay a comb from your cargo in the boat with him
Stand off, with your cap in your hand

The tar takes first, then the oak. You stand in the heat with men whose names you do not know until the strakes fall in. In the morning they rake the rivets out of the ash, and one of them calls you by your boat's name across the river.
An antler comb in its case goes in by his hand. One of the partners nods. A man should arrive combed, he says, wherever it is. They drink to the dead man afterwards, and pour for you without asking.
From where you stand it is a light on the terrace, and then a glow, and then nothing. Your baptised men cross themselves. The others watch to the end.
Under the princess's peace

The fort on the point is timber again behind a new ditch, and the old stone shows black at its foot. A tall grey man in a red cloak, a silver cross on a chain over a coat of eastern cut, walks you the length of the wall before he asks you anything.

A timber fort on a point between two rivers, old blackened stone showing at the foot of its wall: a tall grey man in a red cloak pinned with a gold ring-pin, a silver cross on a chain over an eastern coat, a sword at his side, walking beside a merchant and pointing at the black stone.
You are welcome under the princess's peace. No tenth is taken here. A gift to her house is usual. Tell me first: who is king in England this year?
The Frisian house. Your word last time was true, and I acted on it. Sit by me. What is the Danes' king doing now?
The stone at the foot of this wall is black. Eirik Hakonarson did that. His skald made a poem of it. I have heard the poem.
A law is written at Novgorod. A stranger from over the sea swears alone and is believed. Do not make them regret it while I hold this town.
They want fighting men up the river again, and pay a ship well to bring them. I do not ask what for. Brothers, usually.
A man at Uppsalir went to England and came home with its silver. When I want to know what the English king's pennies are worth, I send to him.
Give him true word of the kings of the west
Ask for the princess's peace on your house
Lay a gift for the princess's house (12 d)
Carry hired fighting men up to the rocks, for the prince's pay (60 d)

He asks after the kings of the west one by one, as a man asks after neighbours, and you tell him what you know and say what you only heard. He marks the difference. It is the only thing, he says, that neither king expects of a man.

He gives it before the men at the gate, in few words. From now the gift at the fort is not asked of your house, the first berth under the wall is yours, and he will hear your suits before any other stranger's.
Twelve pennies' weight, for a princess who has never lived in the town that was her wedding gift. He has it written down by a clerk. He is careful about such things.

Men with shields and no cargo, as many as the boat will hold, who sing going up the river and are sick over the side. They are set down below the rocks and paid for at the fort, in western pennies. Your crew scrub the boat without being told.
